**回答：**

I've got the picture now. Let me confirm what I see in the screenshots and the code, then ask the targeted questions I need to fix the bug properly.

## What I see

**Screenshot 2 (the actual bug):** You searched "espresso" in the drinks search box. One result came back (a coffee image). It's rendered as **one tall card filling the entire left cell of the 5-column `TableLayoutPanel`, stretched from top to bottom of the drinks area** — not the normal ~216px card height, not 5-per-row. The other 4 columns are empty white space.

**Screenshot 1 (the low-fi target you'll send later):** Search bar customer top-left, "CUSTOMER PROFILE" area to its right (not below — noted, this differs from current), drinks search + drink cards with S/M/L/XL in the middle, Order box top-right, Payables box below with promo selection moved into it, Log Sale button below. Sidebar on the right with Transaction/Customers/Feedback. So the current left-column layout (search + profile stacked vertically + promo at bottom of left column) is going to change.

## The bug, from the code

`RefreshProductsPanel()` in the current `TransactionView.cs`:

```csharp
var rows = (products.Count + DrinksColumnCount - 1) / DrinksColumnCount;
_productsGrid.RowCount = rows;
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    _productsGrid.RowStyles.Add(new RowStyle(SizeType.Absolute, 216f));
```

With one product: `rows = (1 + 4) / 5 = 1`. One `RowStyle` of `SizeType.Absolute, 216f` is added. Then:

```csharp
var card = new ProductCardControl(product)
{
    Dock = DockStyle.Fill,     // ← this is the problem
    Margin = new Padding(4),
};
_productsGrid.Controls.Add(card, col, row);
```

The card is `Dock = DockStyle.Fill` in a cell. Normally `Absolute` row height + `Dock.Fill` = the card fills 216px and stops. **But** `TableLayoutPanel` has a well-known quirk: when `RowCount > 0` but not every row has an explicit `RowStyle`, it uses `AutoSize`/`Percent` defaults, and when only one row exists, the panel will grow that row to fill the remaining vertical space if the panel itself is `Dock.Fill` inside a taller parent and there's no competing row.

Actually — more precisely, the specific issue here: `_productsGrid.RowCount = rows` is set, then `RowStyles.Add(...)` is called. But `TableLayoutPanelGrowStyle = AddRows` is also set, and **the `RowCount` setter doesn't necessarily keep `RowStyles.Count` in sync**. In some orderings the panel ends up with `RowCount = 1` but the layout engine treating that single row as the "fill the rest" row because the styles collection and the count disagree, or because when there are fewer rows than `RowCount` and `GrowStyle = AddRows`, the panel appends an implicit auto-sized row.

The observable behavior — one card stretched to full height — is exactly the signature of **a single `Dock.Fill` child in a `TableLayoutPanel` cell whose row resolved to `Percent 100` or `AutoSize` instead of the intended `Absolute 216`**. The `RowStyles.Add` is being applied but the layout pass is not honoring it as the row's effective size, most likely because `RowCount` and `RowStyles.Count` got out of step.

I'm ~85% confident. The remaining 15% is the possibility that `ProductCardControl` itself overrides `OnResize` / sets a minimum height and is expanding its cell — but looking at the bundled `ProductCardControl` from the earlier bundle, it does not; it's a plain `Panel` with `Size = new Size(150, 156)` in the ctor and no height override. So it's the `TableLayoutPanel` row sizing.

## The two candidate fixes

**Fix A (minimal, targeted):** Set `RowCount` *after* adding the row styles, and clear both `RowStyles` and `RowCount` together before rebuilding. Also explicitly set the last row to `Absolute 216` rather than relying on `RowStyles.Add` to be picked up:

```csharp
_productsGrid.Controls.Clear();
_productsGrid.RowStyles.Clear();
_productsGrid.RowCount = 0;

if (_controller is null) return;
var products = _controller.GetProducts(_selectedCategory, _productSearchTxtBx.Text);
var rows = (products.Count + DrinksColumnCount - 1) / DrinksColumnCount;

for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    _productsGrid.RowStyles.Add(new RowStyle(SizeType.Absolute, 216f));
_productsGrid.RowCount = rows;
```

**Fix B (more robust against the whole class of bug):** Drop `Dock.Fill` on the card and use `Anchor = Top | Left | Right` with an explicit `Height = 216` (or whatever the card's intrinsic height is). That way the card cannot stretch vertically regardless of what the row does. Costs you the auto-resize-on-column-width behavior; you'd need to also set `card.Width` in a `CellPaint` or resize handler.

My recommendation: **Fix A first**, verify. If it still stretches, **Fix B** as the belt-and-suspenders. Fix B changes the card contract slightly so it's worth trying A first.

But — I want to be honest — I want to see the actual rendered behavior after Fix A rather than guessing twice.

## What I want to nail down before I write the patch

1. **Which card control is actually in the repo right now?** The bundled `ProductCardControl.cs` from `ai-context-bundle.txt` sets `Size = new Size(150, 156)` and uses `Dock = DockStyle.Bottom` for its internal size row. The current `TransactionView.cs` sets the card's `Dock = DockStyle.Fill` and `Margin = new Padding(4)`, and the row is `Absolute 216f`. **Is `ProductCardControl.cs` still the same as the bundle, or did it change?** If it changed and it now sets `MinimumSize` or overrides `OnLayout`, that changes the diagnosis.
2. **Does the card stretch only when 1 result, or when any number < 5?** Try 2, 3, 4 products and tell me: does the single row of N cards fill the full height too, or only when N=1? This distinguishes "single row gets percent-sized" from "few rows get percent-sized."
3. **Is the `Dock = DockStyle.Fill` on the card required for anything?** i.e., does the card rely on being filled to lay out its S/M/L/XL buttons at the bottom edge? If yes, Fix B needs to preserve that (e.g., set `Anchor = Top|Left|Right` and let the card's internal `Dock.Bottom` size row still work — it will, since the card has its own height).
4. **You said "tables are editable."** Which tables, and editable by whom? Customer grid? Feedback grid? Are we talking in-place cell editing, or "the table data is mutable via the API" (i.e., you can edit a customer and it persists)? This matters for a different reason: if you want editable cells, that interacts with the "some will become card layouts" plan — you generally don't put editable grids inside a card layout. Just want to know the intent so I don't suggest grid-editing scaffolding that you'll rip out.
5. **The low-fi mock in screenshot 1 shows the customer profile to the *right* of the search bar, not below it, and the promo selector moved into the Payables box.** Is that the intended final layout, or is that a rough sketch? Because if it's final, I should be careful not to over-invest in fixing the left column's current layout — the bug fix for the drinks grid is layout-independent, but I want to know how much of what's there is staying.
6. **Unrelated but flagged:** `_pwdSeniorChk.CheckedChanged -= PwdSeniorChk_ProgrammaticReset; ... += PwdSeniorChk_ProgrammaticReset;` — that swap looks like it was meant to suppress the change event during programmatic resets, but it's wired backwards: `-=` then immediately `+=` the *same* no-op handler means the handler is always attached, never suppressed. If the intent was to detach the *real* handler (the one that calls `SetPwdSeniorDiscount`) during programmatic reset, that handler isn't a named method here — it's a lambda in the ctor, so it can't be detached. Is that a known thing you're working around, or a leftover from a refactor? Not blocking the search bug, but I noticed it.

Answer 1–3 and I can hand you a one-line-ish patch for the stretch. Answer 4–5 shapes how much I touch. 6 is just a note.

And yes — I have the use-case context from the plan files (roles, approval chains, dashboard, SMS triggers, menu spec). Nothing there is blocking this bug. If anything changes about the roles once Admin/Manager UI lands, I'll flag it, but for now the Transaction view is a Barista-side surface and I'll treat it as such.

**回答：**

Got it. Let me answer your questions and lay out the fix, then ask the few things I still need.

## The bug, confirmed

Your test — *"the card stretches when it's less than 2 3 4 or something"* — is the smoking gun. Any count that produces **a single row** (1–5 products) stretches. That's not a single-card quirk; that's the row resolving to fill-height instead of `Absolute 216`.

The cause is a documented `TableLayoutPanel` behavior: **when the panel's `RowCount` is set but the layout engine hasn't fully synced `RowStyles`, and there's a single row, that row can resolve as the implicit "fill remaining space" row.** Your code sets `RowCount = rows` *first*, then appends `RowStyles`. There's a window where the two disagree, and with one row there's nothing to anchor against.

The reason it's more visible with 1–5 than with, say, 12 is that with multiple rows, the first N-1 rows absorb the ambiguity; the last row is the one that can grow, and if it grows, it just makes the last row taller. With exactly one row, that one row *is* the last row and takes the whole panel.

## The fix

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein.winforms/Views/Controls/TransactionView.cs`

**Method:** `RefreshProductsPanel()`

**Replace this block:**

```csharp
// Compute the number of rows needed.
var rows = (products.Count + DrinksColumnCount - 1) / DrinksColumnCount;
_productsGrid.RowCount = rows;
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    _productsGrid.RowStyles.Add(new RowStyle(SizeType.Absolute, 216f));   // taller card + margin
```

**With this block:**

```csharp
// Compute the number of rows needed.
var rows = (products.Count + DrinksColumnCount - 1) / DrinksColumnCount;

// Order matters: seed RowStyles BEFORE setting RowCount. If RowCount is set first,
// TableLayoutPanel can resolve a single-row grid's only row as "fill remaining space"
// instead of honoring the Absolute 216 style that arrives a moment later — which is
// exactly the "one result card stretches to full height" bug. Adding the styles first,
// then bumping RowCount to match, keeps the two in sync from the first layout pass.
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    _productsGrid.RowStyles.Add(new RowStyle(SizeType.Absolute, 216f));
_productsGrid.RowCount = rows;
```

That's it. One block swap. Nothing else in the file needs to change for this bug.

**Why this works:** `RowStyles.Add` on a `TableLayoutPanel` whose `RowCount` is still `0` *implicitly increments* `RowCount` to match. So by the time you explicitly assign `_productsGrid.RowCount = rows`, the value already equals `rows` and no re-resolution of the row's size type happens. The engine sees a grid with `rows` rows, all `Absolute 216`, from the first layout pass. No ambiguity, no fill.

## Why I'm not also changing `Dock = DockStyle.Fill` on the card

The card itself has `Size = new Size(150, 200)` in its constructor and computes its internal layout (image rect, size button row) from `Height` in `OnPaint` / `OnResize`. With `Dock.Fill` in a cell that is *actually* 216px tall, the card fills 208px (216 minus 4px margin top and bottom) — close enough to 200 that nothing breaks visually, and the card gets slightly taller as a bonus. If I switch to `Anchor = Top|Left|Right` with a hardcoded `Height`, I'd be fighting the row height and the card would no longer respect the cell. Keep `Dock.Fill`. The row fix is sufficient.

## What I need from you before we move on

1. **Apply the fix and confirm.** Search for `Compute the number of rows needed.` in `TransactionView.cs` — one match. Swap the block. Run the app, search "espresso" (1 result), then "a" or something broad (many results), then a 3–4 result search. Tell me if the single-card case now renders at ~216px tall in the top-left cell.
2. **The low-fi mock you described.** You said: *"the customer profile is now above. Instead of a 3 column layout, it's now the profile covering the whole upper layer, the left panel which is the catalog, and the small right panel which is the payables."* That's a **2-row, 2-column** layout:
   - Row 1: customer profile spanning full width
   - Row 2, col 1: product catalog
   - Row 2, col 2: payables (including promo selector, per the sketch)
   I have not seen the actual mock image yet — the message cut off before the image. **Send the low-fi mock** and I'll plan the restructure. Don't start it until you've confirmed the search bug is fixed, so we don't conflate two changes.
3. **Editable tables clarification.** You said *"editable in terms of the headers are resizable."* That's column resize, not cell editing — good, that's a much smaller ask. Do you also want **cell editing** (double-click a cell, type a new value, save) anywhere specific, or is "editable" only ever going to mean column-width adjustment? The reason I ask: if it's only column resize, there's nothing to build — DataGridView does that by default, and it interacts fine with the future card-layout conversion. If you want real cell editing somewhere, that's a different piece of work and I want to know which grid before I plan around it.
4. **Where does the promo selector live in the new layout?** Your sketch note says "PROMO SELECTION SOMEWHERE HERE" inside the Payables box. Confirm: is the promo button moving from the bottom of the left column into the Payables panel, or is that just a placeholder in the sketch? This affects whether the `_promoMenuBtn` field stays where it is or gets reparented.

That's it. Apply the fix, tell me if the stretch is gone, and send the mock — I'll plan the restructure next.

**回答：**

You're right — my diagnosis was incomplete. The screenshot confirms it: **the last row stretches to fill the remaining vertical space of the panel**, regardless of how many products are in it. That's not a "single row" bug; that's a **TableLayoutPanel final-row fill behavior** that only *looks* like a single-card bug when your search returns fewer than 5 results.

## The real cause

`TableLayoutPanel` has a documented behavior: **if the total height of all rows is less than the panel's client height, the panel expands the last row (or distributes the extra space) to fill the remaining space — even if the last row is `SizeType.Absolute`.** The rule is roughly: the `Absolute`/`Percent`/`AutoSize` styles determine *relative* sizing, but the panel will still stretch to fill itself when `Dock.Fill` gives it more room than the rows need.

Screenshot 1 proves it: 10 cards sit in 2 rows of 5 at ~216px each, then 2 cards in a 3rd row stretch down to fill the rest of the panel. The **row itself** is being stretched, not the cards individually — the cards are `Dock.Fill` so they follow their row.

So my previous patch (reordering `RowStyles.Add` before `RowCount`) helps with the *sync* issue but does **not** fix the *fill-the-panel* issue. The panel is simply taller than `rows × 216`, and it's absorbing the difference into the last row.

## The fix

There are two clean options. **Option A** is what I recommend — small, targeted, no side effects on the rest of the layout.

### Option A — add a spacer row at the bottom

Add one extra row to the grid after the products, with `RowStyle(SizeType.Percent, 100f)`, and leave it empty. The spacer absorbs the leftover vertical space instead of the last product row.

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein.winforms/Views/Controls/TransactionView.cs`

**Method:** `RefreshProductsPanel()`

**Replace this block:**

```csharp
// Compute the number of rows needed.
var rows = (products.Count + DrinksColumnCount - 1) / DrinksColumnCount;

// Order matters: seed RowStyles BEFORE setting RowCount. If RowCount is set first,
// TableLayoutPanel can resolve a single-row grid's only row as "fill remaining space"
// instead of honoring the Absolute 216 style that arrives a moment later — which is
// exactly the "one result card stretches to full height" bug. Adding the styles first,
// then bumping RowCount to match, keeps the two in sync from the first layout pass.
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    _productsGrid.RowStyles.Add(new RowStyle(SizeType.Absolute, 216f));
_productsGrid.RowCount = rows;
```

**With this block:**

```csharp
// Compute the number of rows needed for the products themselves.
var productRows = (products.Count + DrinksColumnCount - 1) / DrinksColumnCount;

// Each product row is a fixed 216px. A trailing spacer row with Percent(100) absorbs
// whatever vertical space is left over in the panel — without it, TableLayoutPanel
// expands the LAST product row to fill the panel, which is what makes a partial final
// row (2 cards after 2 full rows of 5, or a single result) stretch to full height.
for (int r = 0; r < productRows; r++)
    _productsGrid.RowStyles.Add(new RowStyle(SizeType.Absolute, 216f));
_productsGrid.RowStyles.Add(new RowStyle(SizeType.Percent, 100f));

_productsGrid.RowCount = productRows + 1;
```

The card-placement loop below stays exactly as it is — it places cards at `(col, row)` for `row = i / 5`, which never touches the spacer row (the spacer is at index `productRows`, and `i / 5` maxes out at `productRows - 1`). No other change needed.

**Why this works:** the spacer row is the "last" row, so the panel's fill behavior targets the spacer instead of a product row. The spacer has no children, so stretching it is invisible. Product rows stay at their `Absolute 216` heights.

**Trade-off:** the panel will have a small empty area below the last product row when the grid doesn't fill. Given you're moving to a new layout soon, that's fine — but if you want the products to start at the top and just have dead space below (which they will), this is exactly the desired look.

### Option B — cap the panel's height via `AutoSize`

Alternative: set `_productsGrid.AutoSize = true` and `_productsGrid.AutoSizeMode = AutoSizeMode.GrowAndShrink`, and drop `Dock.Fill` to `Dock.Top`. This makes the panel only as tall as its content, so there's nothing to "fill." But this interacts with `AutoScroll = true` in ways that are finicky (scroll works differently when `AutoSize` is on), and it would change how the panel behaves when there are many rows. I'd avoid it unless A fails for some reason.

Go with **A**.

## Now — the mock vs. current

Yes, I can distinguish them clearly. Let me map both:

**Screenshot 2 = your current layout** (the one in the code I already have):

- Left column (260px): customer search + customer profile + "Select a Promo ▾" at the bottom
- Middle: Drinks header + Sort by Category combo + card grid
- Right column (380px): Order / Payables / Log Sale, stacked

**Screenshots 1 & 3 = your low-fi mock** (the target):

- **Row 1 (full width):** `[Search Bar CUSTOMER]` `[CUSTOMER PROFILE]` `[CUSTOMER PROFILE]` — search box on the left, then profile fields to its right. So the customer search *and* the profile sit together across the top.
- **Row 2, left:** a tall narrow panel that is **just the profile info stacked** (the mock labels it "CUSTOMER PROFILE" repeated — clearly a placeholder saying "profile content goes here"). Below it, a `[Select a Promo]` button at the bottom of that same left panel.
- **Row 2, middle:** Drinks + Sort by Category + card grid (3 wide in the mock vs 5 in current — probably just sketch scale).
- **Row 2, right:** Order box on top, Payables box below.
- **Bottom, spanning middle+right:** a full-width `[Log Sale]` bar.

Wait — I want to be careful. Screenshot 1 (the clean "Landing - Staff - POS") shows:

- Top row: `Search Bar CUSTOMER` on the left, then two `CUSTOMER PROFILE` boxes to its right, spanning across.
- Below that, a narrow left panel with `Search Bar DRINKS` at top and then the customer profile placeholder text, then `Select a Promo` at bottom — actually no, looking again, Screenshot 1's left panel top says `Search Bar DRINKS` and the body is the repeated "CUSTOMER PROFILE" text. That's confusing. **Screenshot 3** is clearer: `Search Bar` (customer) top-left, then below it a tall panel of "CUSTOMER PROFILE" placeholders, then `Select a Promo` at the bottom of that left panel. Drinks are middle. Order/Payables right. Log Sale spans bottom-middle-and-right.

So the mock layout is:

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [Search Bar CUSTOMER]   [CUSTOMER PROFILE ....................]  │  ← Row 1: customer area, full width
├───────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬───────────────┤
│                   │                              │  Order        │
│  CUSTOMER         │   Drinks    Sort by Cat.     │               │
│  PROFILE          │   ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐       ├───────────────┤
│  (fields)         │   │card│ │card│ │card│       │  Payables     │
│                   │   └────┘ └────┘ └────┘       │               │
│                   │   ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐       │               │
│                   │   └────┘ └────┘ └────┘       │               │
│                   │                              │               │
│ [Select a Promo]  │                              │               │
│                   ├──────────────────────────────┴───────────────┤
│                   │            [ Log Sale ]                      │  ← spans middle+right
└───────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The customer area is *both* Row 1 (search + profile summary) and Row 2 left (profile detail + promo). That's a bit redundant. I want your read on this before I restructure.

## What I need before I plan the restructure

You said earlier *"tables are editable but some will transition into card layouts so take note of that, will change the layout of transaction view later too."* So I'm holding off on the restructure until the search bug is confirmed fixed. But I do want to nail down the target so I can plan.

1. **Apply the spacer-row fix above, verify the stretch is gone** (test 1-result, 6-result, 12-result searches). Confirm, then we move on.
2. **In the mock — is the top strip (`Search Bar CUSTOMER` + `CUSTOMER PROFILE` box) a summary that stays, or is that the same profile that appears in the left panel?** I.e., are there *two* profile displays, or is the top strip the search + the profile row, and the left panel is something else (order history? points ledger? just "the profile" again as a placeholder)?
3. **Where does the promo button live — left panel bottom, or inside Payables?** Screenshot 3 shows it in the left panel bottom. Screenshot 1's annotation says `PROMO SELECTION SOMEWHERE HERE` inside Payables. Which is the intended final home?
4. **Log Sale placement.** Screenshot 1 shows Log Sale under Payables only (right column). Screenshot 3 shows Log Sale spanning the middle+right width. Which one?
5. **Card grid column count in the mock is 3, current code is 5. Is the mock just sketch-scale, or do you actually want 3 columns?** 3 wide would make much bigger cards; that could be the intent given the mock is wider cards.

Once you confirm the bug fix and answer 2–5, I'll write the restructure plan as a keyword-searchable set of edits, same format as the fix above.

namespace CRM_Morcaffein.Theme
{
    /// <summary>
    /// FlatStyle.Flat buttons don't repaint their fill when Enabled flips false — they just
    /// grey the text and keep whatever BackColor was set, so a disabled primary button still
    /// looks like a brand-colored, seemingly-clickable button. Call TrackEnabledState once
    /// (after the button's "active" colors are set) on any button whose Enabled is toggled at
    /// runtime, and it'll swap to the neutral disabled palette automatically.
    /// </summary>
    public static class ButtonStyler
    {
        public static void TrackEnabledState(Button button)
        {
            var activeBackColor = button.BackColor;
            var activeForeColor = button.ForeColor;

            void Apply()
            {
                button.BackColor = button.Enabled ? activeBackColor : BrandPalette.ButtonDisabledFill;
                button.ForeColor = button.Enabled ? activeForeColor : BrandPalette.ButtonDisabledText;
            }

            button.EnabledChanged += (s, e) => Apply();
            Apply(); // the button may already be disabled at hook-up time (e.g. designer default)
        }
    }
}

            var drinksArea = BuildDrinksArea();
            var rightColumn = BuildOrderColumn();

            lowerRow.Controls.Add(drinksArea);
            lowerRow.Controls.Add(rightColumn);

            // Overlay panel. Not Docked: Dock.Fill on a sibling of an edge-docked column
            // only covers the Fill area, not the edge-docked column. So we use absolute
            // bounds (updated on resize) and BringToFront to sit on top of both drinksArea
            // and rightColumn. Covers Row 2 only — the customer area stays visible so the

            _blockOverlayPanel = new Panel

                BackColor = Color.Transparent,
            };

            _blockOverlayPanel.Controls.Add(_blockOverlayMessageLabel);
            lowerRow.Controls.Add(_blockOverlayPanel);
            _blockOverlayPanel.BringToFront();

            void FitOverlay()
            {
                _blockOverlayPanel.Bounds = new Rectangle(0, 0,
                    lowerRow.ClientSize.Width,
                    lowerRow.ClientSize.Height);
            }
            lowerRow.Resize += (s, e) => FitOverlay();
            FitOverlay();

            tableCardPanel.Controls.Add(lowerRow);
            tableCardPanel.Controls.Add(customerArea);

            cardOuterPanel.Controls.Add(tableCardPanel);
            Controls.Add(cardOuterPanel);
        }

Wait — that comment about add-order is wrong for this specific case. Let me fix before you paste: `Dock.Fill` and `Dock.Left` siblings — the Left one claims its strip first, the Fill one takes the rest. Add-order between them doesn't matter for Left vs Fill. But the profile panel and the error label both being `Dock.Fill` **do** conflict — only one can occupy the Fill region at a time. I'll handle that by keeping both parented and toggling `Visible` (which the existing `RunCustomerSearch` / `SelectCustomerAsync` code already does — it sets `_customerProfilePanel.Visible = false` on error and `true` on success; the error label just gets its `.Text` set).

**But** — the error label needs to be `Dock.Fill` *and* the profile panel needs to be `Dock.Fill`, and WinForms will lay out whichever was added last on top. Since only one is visible at a time, that's fine. I'll correct the comment in the actual patch to say that instead of the wrong "reverse add-order" thing.

Here's the corrected Edit 2 body (use this version, not the one above):

Good — I can see the layout is working. Let me address the four issues carefully, and I'll be explicit about what's a value change vs. a structural change so you can revert anything cleanly.

Before I write the patch, let me confirm the current state from your screenshot so I don't miss anything:

- **Row 1** spans full width. Search box (narrow, left) + profile text ("Janjan Lascuna / Regular Tier • 0 pts") to its right, but the profile's panel extends all the way to the right edge of the card, which is what makes it feel empty. ✅ your read.

- **Promo button** ("Exam Week ▾") is at the bottom of Payables, above Log Sale. ✅
- **Scrolling**: you're right. The `_productsGrid` has `AutoScroll = true`, but the grid is inside `BuildDrinksArea`'s `area` panel, which is inside `lowerRow`, which is inside `tableCardPanel`, which is inside `cardOuterPanel`. `TableLayoutPanel` with `AutoScroll = true` needs the scroll host to *actually* be constrained vertically for the scrollbar to appear. Right now the grid is being given enough height by its parents (because `lowerRow` is `Dock.Fill` and the grid is `Dock.Fill` inside `area`), so the grid never exceeds its own bounds — the products just pile up beyond the visible area with no scrollbar. This is a real bug, not just a setting. I'll fix it as part of this patch.

**Why:** `Dock.Fill` on a textbox forces its height to the parent's inner height. The previous mismatch was because `searchRow` had no fixed height and no padding, so the textbox and the 40px-wide "Go" button were sized independently. Giving `searchRow` a fixed 32px height and making the button square (32×32, equal to row height) means they align on both top and bottom edges. `BorderStyle.FixedSingle` on the textbox draws its own 1px border, so the textbox's *drawn* height is 30px inside a 32px slot — visually flush with the button's 32px. That's the "match" you want.

**Also:** `Width = 300` → `Width = 360` widens the whole search area. Change that one number if you want it wider/narrower.

**Wait — one important correction before you paste this.** `Dock.Left` and `Dock.Fill` siblings do *not* stack the way I wrote it above. If the profile panel is `Dock.Left` and the error label is `Dock.Fill`, they will both occupy the space to the right of the search box, and the Fill one will sit *under* the Left one in z-order, causing the error label to be hidden behind the profile panel or vice versa. Since they're mutually exclusive by `Visible`, that's actually fine — when the profile panel is visible, the error label's `Text` is empty (transparent). When the error label has text, the profile panel is `Visible = false` and the error label fills the space. **So the layout works.** But I want the profile's `Margin` to actually take effect — WinForms honors `Margin` between docked siblings in some cases and not others. To guarantee a 12px gap between the search box and the profile card, add the gap to the profile's `Padding.Left` instead of `Margin`. Let me rewrite:

## EDIT 4 — Restore scrolling on the drinks grid

**File:** `TransactionView.cs`
**Method:** `BuildDrinksArea()`

**This is the real bug.** The `_productsGrid` (a `TableLayoutPanel` with `AutoScroll = true`) never scrolls because its parent chain hands it as much height as it asks for. `AutoScroll` only produces a scrollbar when the control's *content* exceeds the control's *client area* — but if the control itself keeps growing to fit its content (which `Dock.Fill` inside a `Dock.Fill` inside a `Dock.Fill` chain will do), there's nothing to scroll.

**Find (in `BuildDrinksArea`):**

```csharp
            _productsGrid = new TableLayoutPanel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                ColumnCount = DrinksColumnCount,
                RowCount = 0,                       // rows added dynamically by RefreshProductsPanel
                AutoScroll = true,                  // still scrollable if 34 cards don't fit
                Padding = new Padding(12),
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                GrowStyle = TableLayoutPanelGrowStyle.AddRows,
            };
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            _productsGrid = new TableLayoutPanel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                ColumnCount = DrinksColumnCount,
                RowCount = 0,                       // rows added dynamically by RefreshProductsPanel
                AutoScroll = true,                  // still scrollable if 34 cards don't fit
                Padding = new Padding(12),
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                GrowStyle = TableLayoutPanelGrowStyle.AddRows,
                // GrowStyle.AddRows lets the grid append rows past what fits; the parent
                // drinks `area` panel clamps its own height via Dock.Fill, so the grid
                // gets a fixed viewport and AutoScroll produces a real scrollbar. If
                // anything upstream starts AutoSizing to content, the grid will grow
                // again and the scrollbar will disappear — keep the chain fixed-size.
            };
```

That alone doesn't fix it — the comment describes the *condition* for scrolling to work. The actual fix is ensuring the parent chain doesn't grow. Let me trace it:

- `_productsGrid` is `Dock.Fill` inside `area` (the `BuildDrinksArea` return value).
- `area` is `Dock.Fill` inside `lowerRow`.
- `lowerRow` is `Dock.Fill` inside `tableCardPanel`.
- `tableCardPanel` is `Dock.Fill` inside `cardOuterPanel`.
- `cardOuterPanel` is `Dock.Fill` inside `this` (the `TransactionView` UserControl).

All fixed-size parents. So the grid *should* have a fixed viewport. But the screenshot shows no scrollbar. **The likely culprit is `_productsGrid.ResumeLayout()` being called with the `AutoScroll` state mid-flight**, or the `ResumeRedraw`/`SendMessage`/`WM_SETREDRAW` dance interfering with `AutoScroll`'s layout pass. `AutoScroll` on a `TableLayoutPanel` requires a full layout cycle to compute the scroll bounds, and `WM_SETREDRAW = false` around `ResumeLayout()` can cause that pass to be swallowed.

**Fix:** reorder the `finally` block in `RefreshProductsPanel()` so `ResumeLayout()` runs *before* `ResumeRedraw()`, and call `_productsGrid.PerformLayout()` explicitly after both. That forces the scroll-bounds calculation.

**Find (in `RefreshProductsPanel`, the finally block):**

```csharp
            finally
            {
                ResumeRedraw(_productsGrid);
                _productsGrid.ResumeLayout();
            }
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            finally
            {
                // ResumeLayout BEFORE ResumeRedraw: AutoScroll's scroll-bounds calculation
                // runs during the layout pass, and WM_SETREDRAW=false swallows it. An
                // explicit PerformLayout() after both forces the scrollbar to appear on
                // the first render instead of waiting for the next resize.
                _productsGrid.ResumeLayout(performLayout: true);
                ResumeRedraw(_productsGrid);
                _productsGrid.PerformLayout();
            }
```

`ResumeLayout(performLayout: true)` is the overload that forces a layout pass immediately, rather than deferring it. Combined with the explicit `PerformLayout()` after `ResumeRedraw`, the grid recalculates its scrollable area once the visual state is back on.

**One more thing to check after you apply:** if the scrollbar still doesn't appear, the culprit is almost certainly that `AutoScroll` on a `TableLayoutPanel` with `GrowStyle.AddRows` doesn't create a vertical scrollbar reliably — this is a known WinForms quirk. The fallback is to wrap `_productsGrid` in a plain `Panel { AutoScroll = true }` and set `_productsGrid.Dock = DockStyle.Top` inside it, with the grid's height computed as `rows * 216 + padding`. That's a bigger change. **Try the `finally`-block fix first** — if it doesn't work, tell me and I'll give you the wrapper-panel version.

## EDIT A — Customer search: kill the icon, plain text button, proper alignment

**File:** `TransactionView.cs`
**Method:** `BuildCustomerArea()`

The reason it's still misaligned: `Dock.Fill` on the textbox makes it fill the panel's *full* height, and the button is `Dock.Right` — but the row panel itself has no fixed height in the new code, so the textbox is stretching to whatever the row is, while the button is drawing at its own intrinsic height. I'm going to stop fighting `Dock` for this and just **absolute-position both controls** in a fixed-height row. That's the only way to make them match reliably.

**Find the entire searchRow block (from `const int searchRowHeight = 32;` down through `searchRow.Controls.Add(searchBtn);`):**

```csharp
            const int searchRowHeight = 32;

            var searchRow = new Panel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Left,
                Width = 360,
                Height = searchRowHeight,
                Padding = new Padding(0),
            };

            var searchBtn = new Button
            {
                Text = "🔍",
                Width = searchRowHeight,
                Dock = DockStyle.Right,
                FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat,
                BackColor = BrandPalette.ButtonSecondaryFill,
                ForeColor = BrandPalette.ButtonSecondaryText,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(11f),
                Cursor = Cursors.Hand,
                Padding = new Padding(0),
                TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleCenter,
            };
            searchBtn.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 0;
            searchBtn.Click += (s, e) => RunCustomerSearch();

            _customerSearchTxtBx = new TextBox
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                PlaceholderText = "Customer ID or phone",
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10f),
                BorderStyle = BorderStyle.FixedSingle,
            };

            _customerSearchTxtBx.KeyDown += (s, e) =>
            {
                if (e.KeyCode == Keys.Enter) { RunCustomerSearch(); e.SuppressKeyPress = true; }
            };

            _customerSearchTxtBx.KeyPress += (s, e) =>
            {
                // Only digits allowed — the POS search accepts Customer ID or phone, both numeric.
                if (!char.IsControl(e.KeyChar) && !char.IsDigit(e.KeyChar))
                    e.Handled = true;
            };

            searchRow.Controls.Add(_customerSearchTxtBx);
            searchRow.Controls.Add(searchBtn);
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // Fixed-height row, absolute-positioned children. Dock.Fill on the textbox made
            // it stretch to the row's full height while the button drew at its own intrinsic
            // height — the two could never match. Pinning both to the same y/height is the
            // only reliable way to align them.
            const int searchRowHeight = 34;
            const int searchButtonWidth = 80;

            var searchRow = new Panel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Left,
                Width = 360,
                Height = searchRowHeight,
                Padding = new Padding(0),
            };

            _customerSearchTxtBx = new TextBox
            {
                Location = new Point(0, 0),
                Width = searchRow.Width - searchButtonWidth,
                Height = searchRowHeight,
                PlaceholderText = "Customer ID or phone",
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10.5f),
                BorderStyle = BorderStyle.FixedSingle,
            };

            _customerSearchTxtBx.KeyDown += (s, e) =>
            {
                if (e.KeyCode == Keys.Enter) { RunCustomerSearch(); e.SuppressKeyPress = true; }
            };

            _customerSearchTxtBx.KeyPress += (s, e) =>
            {
                // Only digits allowed — the POS search accepts Customer ID or phone, both numeric.
                if (!char.IsControl(e.KeyChar) && !char.IsDigit(e.KeyChar))
                    e.Handled = true;
            };

            var searchBtn = new Button
            {
                Text = "Search",
                Location = new Point(searchRow.Width - searchButtonWidth, 0),
                Width = searchButtonWidth,
                Height = searchRowHeight,
                FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat,
                BackColor = BrandPalette.ButtonSecondaryFill,
                ForeColor = BrandPalette.ButtonSecondaryText,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(9f),
                Cursor = Cursors.Hand,
                Padding = new Padding(0),
                TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleCenter,
            };
            searchBtn.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 0;
            searchBtn.Click += (s, e) => RunCustomerSearch();

            searchRow.Controls.Add(_customerSearchTxtBx);
            searchRow.Controls.Add(searchBtn);
```

**Why this works when Dock didn't:** both controls now have `Location.Y = 0` and `Height = 34`. The textbox and the button are literally the same rectangle height. The textbox draws its `FixedSingle` border inside those 34px, so its visible box is 32px — 1px inset on top, 1px on bottom. The button fills all 34. Visually they share the same top and bottom line. If it still looks off by a pixel, that's the textbox's border inset, and the fix is to set the button to `Height = 32` and `Location.Y = 1` — but try the above first.

**Also:** the row is now `Width = 360`, textbox is `360 - 80 = 280px`, button is `80px`. Change those two constants at the top of the block if you want different proportions.

**File:** `TransactionView.cs`
**Method:** `BuildCustomerArea()`

**Find:**

```csharp
            _customerProfilePanel = new Panel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Left,
                Width = 340,
                Visible = false,
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                BorderStyle = BorderStyle.FixedSingle,
                Padding = new Padding(24, 8, 12, 8),   // 24px left = visual gap from the search box

```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // No background, no border — the panel itself is transparent and only the
            // content (name + tier/points) is emphasized. Reads as "this is who you're
            // serving" without a hard-edged box competing with the search field.
            _customerProfilePanel = new Panel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Left,
                Width = 320,
                Visible = false,
                BackColor = Color.Transparent,
                Padding = new Padding(24, 4, 8, 4),    // 24px left = visual gap from the search box
            };

            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Top,
                Height = 26,

                Dock = DockStyle.Top,
                Height = 22,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(9.5f),

                BackColor = Color.Transparent,
            };

            _customerProfilePanel.Controls.Add(_customerProfileNameLabel);
```

**One WinForms gotcha you must know:** a `Panel` with `BackColor = Color.Transparent` inside a parent that has a solid `BackColor` (the customer area's `SurfaceCard` tint) will *not* actually be transparent unless the parent supports transparent children. `Panel` does support transparent `BackColor` — it inherits the parent's painted background. But the two child `Label`s also need `BackColor = Color.Transparent` (added above), otherwise they'll each paint a small opaque box. That's why I set it on both labels.

**What changes visually:** the box and border are gone. The name text is now brand brown (`Brand`), which is the "highlight" you asked for. The tier/points line stays muted. The whole profile block just floats in the tinted strip to the right of the search box.

**If the brand-brown name is too much**, change `ForeColor = BrandPalette.Brand` to `BrandPalette.NeutralText` and instead consider a subtle highlight — but I'd try the brand color first, it's exactly the "intentional" look you described.

## EDIT C — Drinks search slowness

I can't write this fix without seeing `TransactionController.GetProducts`. Two things I can do blind, but I'd rather do the right one:

**Blind fix (safe, helps regardless):** debounce the search box so it doesn't fire `RefreshProductsPanel()` on every keystroke. Add a `System.Windows.Forms.Timer` that waits ~250ms after the last keystroke before refreshing.

**Find:**

```csharp
            _productSearchTxtBx.TextChanged += (s, e) => RefreshProductsPanel();
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // Debounce: only refresh the grid after the user has stopped typing for 250ms.
            // Rebuilding the whole TableLayoutPanel on every keystroke is expensive enough
            // to be visible as lag on a 40-product catalog.
            _productSearchDebounce = new System.Windows.Forms.Timer { Interval = 250 };
            _productSearchDebounce.Tick += (s, e) =>
            {
                _productSearchDebounce.Stop();
                RefreshProductsPanel();
            };
            _productSearchTxtBx.TextChanged += (s, e) =>
            {
                _productSearchDebounce.Stop();
                _productSearchDebounce.Start();
            };
```

**And add the field** near the other fields at the top of the class:

```csharp
        private System.Windows.Forms.Timer _productSearchDebounce = null!;
```

That will cut the perceived slowness *if* the slowness is from repeated rebuilds. **But** if `GetProducts` is hitting the network or doing heavy work, the debounce just delays each expensive call — you'd still feel it once. That's why I want the controller.

## EDIT D — The scrollbar (still not fixed)

You're right, and my previous fix was wrong — I assumed the `finally` reorder would do it, but the screenshot proves it didn't. Here's the real problem and the real fix.

`AutoScroll = true` on a `TableLayoutPanel` **does not reliably produce a scrollbar when the panel is `Dock.Fill`**, because WinForms gives `Dock.Fill` controls "whatever height the parent has" and the TableLayoutPanel's scroll logic compares content height to client height *during layout*, before the parent has finalized sizes. It works sometimes and not others. This is a long-standing WinForms quirk.

**The reliable pattern is: wrap the grid in a scrolling host panel.**

**Step 1 — in `BuildDrinksArea()`, find:**

```csharp
            _productsGrid = new TableLayoutPanel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                ColumnCount = DrinksColumnCount,
                RowCount = 0,                       // rows added dynamically by RefreshProductsPanel
                AutoScroll = true,                  // still scrollable if 34 cards don't fit
                Padding = new Padding(12),
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                GrowStyle = TableLayoutPanelGrowStyle.AddRows,
                // GrowStyle.AddRows lets the grid append rows past what fits; the parent
                // drinks `area` panel clamps its own height via Dock.Fill, so the grid
                // gets a fixed viewport and AutoScroll produces a real scrollbar. If
                // anything upstream starts AutoSizing to content, the grid will grow
                // again and the scrollbar will disappear — keep the chain fixed-size.
            };
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // A plain Panel hosts the scroll. TableLayoutPanel's own AutoScroll is unreliable
            // when it's Dock.Fill inside a Dock.Fill chain — the scrollbar only appears if
            // the grid's own height exceeds its client area, which Dock.Fill prevents. The
            // wrapper gives us a control whose ONLY job is scrolling, and the grid lives
            // inside it at its natural height (Dock.Top + explicit Height, recomputed in
            // RefreshProductsPanel).
            _productsScrollHost = new Panel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                AutoScroll = true,
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                Padding = new Padding(0),
            };

            _productsGrid = new TableLayoutPanel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Top,               // NOT Fill — height is set explicitly in RefreshProductsPanel
                ColumnCount = DrinksColumnCount,
                RowCount = 0,
                AutoScroll = false,                 // the host scrolls, not the grid
                Padding = new Padding(12),
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                GrowStyle = TableLayoutPanelGrowStyle.AddRows,
            };

            for (int i = 0; i < DrinksColumnCount; i++)
                _productsGrid.ColumnStyles.Add(new ColumnStyle(SizeType.Percent, 100f / DrinksColumnCount));

            _productsScrollHost.Controls.Add(_productsGrid);
```

**Step 2 — remove the old column-styles loop that's now duplicated below this block.** In the current code there's a block:

```csharp
            // Equal-width columns for the cards.
            for (int i = 0; i < DrinksColumnCount; i++)
                _productsGrid.ColumnStyles.Add(new ColumnStyle(SizeType.Percent, 100f / DrinksColumnCount));

            area.Controls.Add(_productsGrid);
            area.Controls.Add(header);
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            area.Controls.Add(_productsScrollHost);
            area.Controls.Add(header);
```

(Columns are now added in the block above, next to the grid's construction.)

**Step 3 — add the field** near the other fields:

```csharp
        private Panel _productsScrollHost = null!;
```

**Step 4 — in `RefreshProductsPanel()`, after building the rows, set the grid's height explicitly.** Find the end of the card-placement loop:

```csharp
                    var row = i / DrinksColumnCount;
                    var col = i % DrinksColumnCount;
                    _productsGrid.Controls.Add(card, col, row);
                }
            }
            finally
            {
                // ResumeLayout BEFORE ResumeRedraw: AutoScroll's scroll-bounds calculation
                // runs during the layout pass, and WM_SETREDRAW=false swallows it. An
                // explicit PerformLayout() after both forces the scrollbar to appear on
                // the first render instead of waiting for the next resize.
                _productsGrid.ResumeLayout(performLayout: true);
                ResumeRedraw(_productsGrid);
                _productsGrid.PerformLayout();
            }
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
                    var row = i / DrinksColumnCount;
                    var col = i % DrinksColumnCount;
                    _productsGrid.Controls.Add(card, col, row);
                }

                // Dock.Top doesn't grow with content, so set the height to exactly what the
                // rows need. The scroll host compares this against its own client height and
                // shows a scrollbar when the grid is taller.
                var gridHeight = productRows * 216 + _productsGrid.Padding.Vertical;
                _productsGrid.Height = Math.Max(gridHeight, _productsScrollHost.ClientSize.Height);
            }
            finally
            {
                ResumeRedraw(_productsGrid);
                _productsGrid.ResumeLayout(performLayout: true);
                _productsScrollHost.PerformLayout();
            }
```

**What this changes:** the grid is no longer trying to scroll itself. The wrapper panel does the scrolling, and the grid reports its true content height (`productRows * 216 + padding`). When there are more rows than fit, the wrapper's `AutoScroll` produces a real scrollbar. This is the standard WinForms workaround and it's reliable.

**One caveat:** the scrollbar will appear *inside* the host panel, on the right edge of the drinks area. If your cards have a right margin, the scrollbar sits just outside them — that's normal and fine.

**回答：**

Perfect — now I have the full picture. `GetProducts` is pure in-memory LINQ over `_allProducts`. It's **fast**. So the slowness is not there.

## Where the slowness actually is

It's in `RefreshProductsPanel()` in `TransactionView.cs`. On every keystroke, that method:

1. Clears the entire `TableLayoutPanel` (`Controls.Clear()`, `RowStyles.Clear()`).
2. Calls `GetProducts` (fast, in-memory).
3. **Reads every matched product's image bytes from disk** in the preload loop.
4. Constructs a brand-new `ProductCardControl` for every result.
5. Rebuilds the whole grid's row styles and re-adds every card.

For a broad search ("a", "m", etc.) that's 40 products × (1 disk read + 1 control allocation + 1 paint setup). Every keystroke. That's the lag.

The **image preload loop is the main offender** — it does `File.ReadAllBytes` on every image on every keystroke, and it's completely redundant because `ProductCardControl.TryLoadImage` loads on demand and caches per-card instance. The only reason the loop exists is to "warm" the disk cache, but since the cards are rebuilt every keystroke, the warm cache doesn't help — and the reads themselves cost more than the painting they were meant to speed up.

The **second offender** is the full teardown/rebuild. For a 40-product catalog that's borderline okay, but combined with the disk reads it's noticeable.

## Three fixes, all in `TransactionView.cs`

The controller needs **no change** — you were right to ask, but the answer is it's clean.

---

### EDIT 1 — Delete the redundant image preload loop

**File:** `TransactionView.cs`
**Method:** `RefreshProductsPanel()`

**Find this block:**

```csharp
                // Preload all images for this batch before building cards.
                foreach (var product in products)
                {
                    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(product.LocalImagePath))
                    {
                        var fullPath = Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, product.LocalImagePath);
                        if (File.Exists(fullPath))
                        {
                            try { _ = File.ReadAllBytes(fullPath); } catch { }
                        }
                    }
                }
```

**Delete it entirely** (the whole `foreach` block plus the comment, leaving the blank line before "Compute the number of rows needed" removed too so the code flows straight from `products` to the row computation).

**Why:** `ProductCardControl.TryLoadImage` already loads and caches each image on first paint. The preload loop reads the same bytes a second time, on every keystroke, for every matched product, and the benefit (disk cache warmth) is destroyed the moment the cards are rebuilt and disposed. Removing it will cut a meaningful chunk of the per-keystroke cost.

---

### EDIT 2 — Debounce the search box

**File:** `TransactionView.cs`

**Add a field** near the other private fields at the top of the class (e.g. right after `private string _selectedCategory = string.Empty;`):

```csharp
        private System.Windows.Forms.Timer _productSearchDebounce = null!;
```

**Find (inside `BuildDrinksArea()`):**

```csharp
            _productSearchTxtBx.TextChanged += (s, e) => RefreshProductsPanel();
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // Debounce: rebuild the grid only after the user has stopped typing for 200ms.
            // Full teardown + rebuild of a 40-card TableLayoutPanel on every keystroke is
            // the reason typing in this box felt laggy. 200ms is short enough to feel
            // instant when you pause, long enough that a burst of keystrokes coalesces
            // into a single rebuild.
            _productSearchDebounce = new System.Windows.Forms.Timer { Interval = 200 };
            _productSearchDebounce.Tick += (s, e) =>
            {
                _productSearchDebounce.Stop();
                RefreshProductsPanel();
            };
            _productSearchTxtBx.TextChanged += (s, e) =>
            {
                _productSearchDebounce.Stop();
                _productSearchDebounce.Start();
            };
```

**Note:** `_productSearchDebounce` starts ticking only after the first `TextChanged`; the constructor's initial `RefreshProductsPanel()` call (if there is one) is unaffected. `TransactionView` has no `Dispose` override currently — `Timer` will be disposed with the control's handle teardown, but if you want to be tidy, add:

```csharp
        protected override void Dispose(bool disposing)
        {
            if (disposing) _productSearchDebounce?.Dispose();
            base.Dispose(disposing);
        }
```

That's optional; skipping it won't cause a leak in practice for a control that lives for the app lifetime, but it's correct.

---

### EDIT 3 — Skip the rebuild when the result set hasn't changed

This is the defensive layer. The debounce alone helps, but if a user types "esp", backspaces to "es", then types "p" again, they're rebuilding the same result set. The signature check already exists in the method:

```csharp
            var signature = $"{_selectedCategory}|{_productSearchTxtBx.Text}";
            if (signature == _lastProductFilterSignature && _productsGrid.Controls.Count > 0)
                return;
```

But it's keyed on the **query string**, not the **result set**. Two different queries can produce the same result set (e.g. "matcha" vs "MATCHA"), and — more importantly — the signature check is only useful when the exact same string is re-entered. It doesn't help during the "esp → es → esp" flow because each intermediate state writes a new signature and blows away `_lastProductFilterSignature`.

Leave it. It's doing its job for the case it was written for, and adding result-set comparison would mean hashing the filtered list, which is more complexity than the win justifies. **The debounce is the real fix.** The signature check stays as-is.

You said "the panel is still not changed." But in your screenshot from the last message, the search box was **still** showing the 🔍 icon button, not "Search". And the profile was still a bordered box. So **Edits A and B from two turns ago either weren't applied, or were applied and then overwritten by a later paste.**

2. `BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,` immediately followed by `BorderStyle = BorderStyle.FixedSingle,` **inside `_customerProfilePanel`'s initializer** — should **not** be there if Edit B landed. Should be `BackColor = Color.Transparent,` with no `BorderStyle`.

If any of those don't match what I described, the edit didn't take. Paste me the current `BuildCustomerArea()` and `BuildDrinksArea()` methods (or just the whole file again) and I'll re-issue the edits against what's actually there.

### Question 2: The scrollbar — my Edit D was incomplete

I need to own this: **I gave you a scroll fix that doesn't work as written.** Re-reading my Edit D, the height-setting line is:

```csharp
var gridHeight = productRows * 216 + _productsGrid.Padding.Vertical;
_productsGrid.Height = Math.Max(gridHeight, _productsScrollHost.ClientSize.Height);
```

That `Math.Max` is the bug. It clamps the grid height to **at least** the host's client height — which means when the content is taller than the viewport, the grid grows (fine), but when the content is *shorter*, the grid still fills the host, and **when the content is taller, `ClientSize.Height` inside the `RefreshProductsPanel` call may be stale or zero** depending on when it's read. On the first paint, `_productsScrollHost.ClientSize.Height` is likely 0 or the pre-layout value, so `Math.Max(gridHeight, 0)` = `gridHeight`. That part is actually correct. So the grid *should* grow.

But the wrapper panel's `AutoScroll` won't produce a scrollbar unless the grid's **`Top` + `Height` exceeds the host's client height at layout time**. And here's the thing I missed: `_productsGrid` is `Dock.Top`. When a child is `Dock.Top` inside an `AutoScroll` panel, WinForms treats the **docked child as part of the scrollable content** — but only if the child's height is set explicitly **and** the host's `AutoScrollMinSize` or the child's bottom edge exceeds the host's client area. In practice, `Dock.Top` children inside `AutoScroll` panels are notorious for not triggering the scrollbar because the dock manager keeps resetting the child's width to the host width and treating its height as "whatever it needs to be" — which, for a `Dock.Top` control, is not always the explicit `Height` you set.

**The reliable pattern** is `Dock.None` (absolute positioning) on the grid inside the wrapper — set `Location = (0, 0)` and `Width = host.ClientSize.Width - scrollbarWidth`, `Height = gridHeight` explicitly, and update those on the host's `Resize`. That's how the `CartLineControl` in the Order box already does it — absolute positioning, no Dock, update on resize.

Let me re-issue the scroll fix properly.

## EDIT D (revised) — Scroll host with absolute-positioned grid

**File:** `TransactionView.cs`

### Step 1 — Field

Confirm this field exists near the top (from the previous Edit D):

```csharp
        private Panel _productsScrollHost = null!;
```

If it doesn't, add it.

### Step 2 — `BuildDrinksArea()`: construct the host and grid

**Find:**

```csharp

            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                AutoScroll = true,
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                Padding = new Padding(0),
            };

            _productsGrid = new TableLayoutPanel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Top,               // NOT Fill — height is set explicitly in RefreshProductsPanel
                ColumnCount = DrinksColumnCount,
                RowCount = 0,
                AutoScroll = false,                 // the host scrolls, not the grid
                Padding = new Padding(12),
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                GrowStyle = TableLayoutPanelGrowStyle.AddRows,

```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            _productsScrollHost = new Panel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                AutoScroll = true,
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
            };

            _productsGrid = new TableLayoutPanel
            {
                // ABSOLUTE positioning, no Dock. A Dock.Top child inside an AutoScroll panel
                // gets its height re-managed by the dock engine, which is why the scrollbar
                // never appeared. Location + explicit Width/Height (set in
                // RefreshProductsPanel and on host resize) is what CartLineControl already
                // does for the same reason — it's the only reliable way to get an AutoScroll
                // panel to actually scroll.
                Location = new Point(0, 0),
                ColumnCount = DrinksColumnCount,
                RowCount = 0,
                AutoScroll = false,
                Padding = new Padding(12),
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                GrowStyle = TableLayoutPanelGrowStyle.AddRows,
            };

            for (int i = 0; i < DrinksColumnCount; i++)
                _productsGrid.ColumnStyles.Add(new ColumnStyle(SizeType.Percent, 100f / DrinksColumnCount));

            // Keep the grid's width synced to the host, minus the scrollbar strip when one
            // is showing. Height is set in RefreshProductsPanel where the row count is known.
            _productsScrollHost.Resize += (s, e) => SyncProductsGridWidth();
            _productsScrollHost.Controls.Add(_productsGrid);
```

### Step 3 — Add the width-sync helper

Add this method to the class, next to the other helpers (e.g. right after `ShowCartStatus`):

```csharp
        private void SyncProductsGridWidth()
        {
            if (_productsScrollHost is null || _productsGrid is null)
                return;

            var hostWidth = _productsScrollHost.ClientSize.Width;
            if (hostWidth <= 0) return;

            // If a vertical scrollbar is showing, its width is already excluded from
            // ClientSize. If it isn't showing yet but will be (because the grid is taller
            // than the host), the first layout pass excludes it too. Either way, using
            // ClientSize.Width is correct — the grid fills the visible area, and the host
            // re-fires Resize when the scrollbar appears or disappears.
            _productsGrid.Width = hostWidth;
        }
```

### Step 4 — `RefreshProductsPanel()`: set grid height after building rows

**Find (the tail of the method, inside the `try`, after the card-placement loop):**

```csharp
                    var row = i / DrinksColumnCount;
                    var col = i % DrinksColumnCount;
                    _productsGrid.Controls.Add(card, col, row);
                }

                // Dock.Top doesn't grow with content, so set the height to exactly what the
                // rows need. The scroll host compares this against its own client height and
                // shows a scrollbar when the grid is taller.
                var gridHeight = productRows * 216 + _productsGrid.Padding.Vertical;
                _productsGrid.Height = Math.Max(gridHeight, _productsScrollHost.ClientSize.Height);
            }
            finally
            {
                ResumeRedraw(_productsGrid);
                _productsGrid.ResumeLayout(performLayout: true);
                _productsScrollHost.PerformLayout();
            }
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
                    var row = i / DrinksColumnCount;
                    var col = i % DrinksColumnCount;
                    _productsGrid.Controls.Add(card, col, row);
                }

                // Absolute-positioned grid: set both dimensions explicitly. Width from the
                // host (minus scrollbar if present), height from the actual row count. When
                // this height exceeds the host's client height, AutoScroll on the host shows
                // a real scrollbar.
                SyncProductsGridWidth();
                _productsGrid.Height = productRows * 216 + _productsGrid.Padding.Vertical + _productsGrid.Padding.Top;
            }
            finally
            {
                ResumeRedraw(_productsGrid);
                _productsGrid.ResumeLayout(performLayout: true);
                _productsScrollHost.PerformLayout();
            }
```

**Note on the height formula:** `Padding.Vertical` is `Top + Bottom`. I added `Padding.Top` again on top of it — that's wrong. Use this instead:

```csharp
                _productsGrid.Height = productRows * 216 + _productsGrid.Padding.Top + _productsGrid.Padding.Bottom;
```

That's `Padding.Vertical` written explicitly, which is what you want. Same number. I just want to be clear so you don't end up double-counting.

### Step 5 — Trigger the width-sync on first show

`Resize` fires when the host first sizes, but if the host is constructed and sized before `Resize` is wired (which it is — `BuildDrinksArea` runs, then the layout pass sizes the host), the first `Resize` will fire anyway on the initial layout pass, so `SyncProductsGridWidth` runs once. If for some reason the grid appears at width 0 on first paint, add a one-shot call at the end of the constructor:

```csharp
            SyncProductsGridWidth();
```

right after `RefreshSummary();` in the parameterless constructor. Harmless if it runs early.

## Why this version actually scrolls

The grid is no longer docked. Its `Height` is set to the literal pixel height of `productRows * 216 + padding`. The host is `AutoScroll = true` and its `ClientSize.Height` is fixed by the layout chain (drinks area → header + host fill). When `grid.Height > host.ClientSize.Height`, the host's scroll machinery kicks in and shows a vertical scrollbar. When `grid.Height <= host.ClientSize.Height`, no scrollbar. That's the standard, documented, reliable pattern.

The previous version's `Dock.Top` was the failure — the dock manager was overwriting the grid's height on every layout pass, which meant it was always exactly the host's height and never exceeded it, so `AutoScroll` had nothing to scroll.
