**回答：**

You're right — the modal is 540 wide, the drawer/container clips it, and the Edit button is being pushed off or covered because `PositionActionButtons` runs before the panel has its final width. Fix it by laying out left-to-right at fixed positions inside the action row's own coordinate space, and by forcing the layout to run after the form is shown. No diagnostics, no guesses — here's the patch.

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein/Views/Forms/FrmCampaignDetail.cs` — wherever the file lives. Same file you just pasted.

## Patch 1 — replace `PositionActionButtons` with fixed left-to-right layout

**Search for:**

```csharp
        private void PositionActionButtons(Panel row)
        {
            // Layout strategy: primary/Create/Save on the far RIGHT (a common dialog
            // convention), then Edit/Activate/Deactivate/Cancel/Close stepping LEFT in
            // the visual order they should appear. Only visible buttons participate.
            //
            // The method is idempotent — safe to call on every resize, every mode change,
            // and after the form is first shown. The prior version relied on the panel's
            // ClientSize being correct at construction time, which it isn't; that's why
            // buttons overlapped.

            var width = row.ClientSize.Width;
            if (width <= 0) return;   // not laid out yet; a later Resize will call us again

            const int gap = 8;
            const int rightInset = 16;
            const int topY = 8;

            // Collect visible buttons in the order we want them packed right-to-left.
            // This list drives the visual order: primary on the right, then Edit, then
            // Activate/Deactivate, then Cancel/Close.
            var ordered = new[]
            {
                _primaryBtn,
                _editBtn,
                _activateBtn,
                _deactivateBtn,
                _cancelBtn,
                _closeBtn,
            };

            var rightEdge = width - rightInset;

            foreach (var btn in ordered)
            {
                if (!btn.Visible) continue;

                btn.Left = rightEdge - btn.Width;
                btn.Top = topY;
                rightEdge -= btn.Width + gap;
            }
        }
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
        /// <summary>
        /// Places the visible action buttons left-to-right at fixed offsets inside the
        /// row. Deliberately does NOT depend on the row's ClientSize — this runs during
        /// the form's Load event, before docking has settled, and earlier attempts to
        /// compute positions from ClientSize pushed buttons off the right edge (or behind
        /// each other) because the row reported a stale or zero width at that moment.
        ///
        /// Layout: buttons are laid out in visual order from x=16 onward, rightward.
        /// Whatever fits, fits; the row's Width is generous enough for every combination
        /// of visible buttons, which is why fixed offsets are safe here.
        ///
        /// Visual order (left → right):
        ///   Close / Cancel  |  Deactivate  |  Activate  |  Edit  |  Create/Save
        /// Destructive (Deactivate) sits well away from the confirm action (Create/Save)
        /// to avoid mis-clicks.
        /// </summary>
        private void PositionActionButtons(Panel row)
        {
            const int leftInset = 16;
            const int gap = 8;
            const int topY = 8;

            var ordered = new[]
            {
                _closeBtn,
                _cancelBtn,
                _deactivateBtn,
                _activateBtn,
                _editBtn,
                _primaryBtn,
            };

            var x = leftInset;

            foreach (var btn in ordered)
            {
                if (!btn.Visible) continue;

                btn.Left = x;
                btn.Top = topY;
                x += btn.Width + gap;
            }
        }
```

## Patch 2 — run `PositionActionButtons` after the form is shown, not before

`ApplyMode()` is called from the constructor, and `BuildLayout()` also calls `PositionActionButtons` directly. Both run before the form has settled its layout. Add a `Load` hook that re-runs positioning once the form is actually visible.

**In the constructor, search for:**

```csharp
            BuildLayout();

            if (initialMode == Mode.Create)
                PopulateEmptyForm();
            else
                PopulateFromExisting();

            ApplyMode();
        }
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            BuildLayout();

            if (initialMode == Mode.Create)
                PopulateEmptyForm();
            else
                PopulateFromExisting();

            ApplyMode();

            // Re-run button positioning once the form is shown. ApplyMode and BuildLayout
            // run before docking settles, so their button positions may be off. Load fires
            // after ClientSize is final, guaranteeing a correct layout.
            Load += (s, e) => PositionActionButtons(_actionRow);
        }
```

## Patch 3 — remove the two reflow hooks that were firing with a stale row width

**Search for:**

```csharp
            // Position all buttons right-aligned on the row whenever it resizes.
            row.Resize += (s, e) => PositionActionButtons(row);

            // Also re-run on the FORM's resize — the row's Resize fires when the row
            // itself changes size, but the initial layout pass may not trigger it in
            // every case (e.g. before the modal is shown).
            Resize += (s, e) => PositionActionButtons(row);

            return row;
        }
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // No resize hooks — the modal is FixedDialog, the row is fixed height, and
            // buttons are laid out at fixed left-to-right offsets. PositionActionButtons
            // is called once from the form's Load handler after ClientSize settles.

            return row;
        }
```

## Patch 4 — one more thing: the View panel clips its content

Looking at your screenshot, the View panel is 540-wide with 24px form padding each side, so the panel is ~492 wide. `RefreshViewPanel` places labels at `labelX = 18` and `valueX = 180`, with `MaximumSize` on the value label set to `_viewPanel.Width - valueX - 18`. **At the moment `RefreshViewPanel` runs, `_viewPanel.Width` may still be the default (0 or small)**, because it's called from `ApplyMode()` in the constructor. That means the value labels get a tiny `MaximumSize`, and long values (like "September 15, 2026") get clipped to nothing.

Fix: don't constrain the value label width with `MaximumSize` at all, and let the form be wider than 540 so there's room. Or — re-run `RefreshViewPanel` on `Load` too.

Simpler fix: **bump the modal's ClientSize to 600 wide**, so even with a stale width during construction, there's headroom.

**Search for:**

```csharp
            ClientSize = new Size(540, 640);
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            ClientSize = new Size(600, 640);
```

Also, **in `RefreshViewPanel`, drop the `MaximumSize` line** — with a 600-wide form and valueX=180, values have 400px of room, plenty for any campaign field.

**Search for:**

```csharp
                _viewPanel.Controls.Add(new Label
                {
                    Text = value,
                    Location = new Point(valueX, y),
                    MaximumSize = new Size(_viewPanel.Width - valueX - 18, 0),
                    AutoSize = true,
                    Font = valueFont ?? BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(9.5f),
                    ForeColor = valueColor ?? BrandPalette.NeutralText,
                });
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
                _viewPanel.Controls.Add(new Label
                {
                    Text = value,
                    Location = new Point(valueX, y),
                    AutoSize = true,
                    Font = valueFont ?? BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(9.5f),
                    ForeColor = valueColor ?? BrandPalette.NeutralText,
                });
```

And also re-run `RefreshViewPanel` on `Load`:

**In the `Load` hook you're adding in Patch 2, expand it:**

**Replace:**

```csharp
            Load += (s, e) => PositionActionButtons(_actionRow);
```

**With:**

```csharp
            Load += (s, e) =>
            {
                PositionActionButtons(_actionRow);
                if (_mode == Mode.View) RefreshViewPanel();
            };
```

That re-lays the labels once `_viewPanel` has its real width.

Good, that's a clear re-order. Let me restate the plan so we're on the same page, then scope M4 (customer editing + Admin review) since that's next.

## Revised roadmap

1. **M4 — Customer editing + Admin review (chain B2).** Now.
2. **M4b — Campaign creation approval (chain B3).** After M4.
3. **M4c — More complex campaign types** (B1T1, per-10-purchases, support-ticket coupon). After M4b. Since you said earlier we'd hold these until the base campaign flow was approved and working — that's now.

5. **M6 — SMS.** After M5.

I'll keep the "one patch per prompt, wait for confirmation" cadence. Before M4 goes out, I need to settle a handful of design decisions, same as I did for M1, M2, M3.

## M4 — Customer editing + Admin review (B2)

**What chain B2 is, per your plan files:**

> CUSTOMER EDITS — APPLIES IMMEDIATELY, ADMIN CAN REVERSE
> Manager edits a customer record. The change is written to the DB immediately (visible to everyone). Simultaneously a review request is queued for Admin. Admin can approve (no-op — already applied) or reject, in which case the record REVERTS to its previous value.

So three things have to exist:

- **The edit itself.** Already built in the Manager's Customers drawer (M1). When a Manager saves an edit, the API currently just applies it. **It needs to also write a review-queue row capturing the previous values.**
- **A new entity** — a "pending customer edit review" row. Let me call it `CustomerEditReview`. Columns: `CustomerEditReviewId`, `CustomerId`, `RequestedBy` (employee ID), `RequestedAt`, `Status` (`Pending` / `Approved` / `Reverted`), `DecidedBy`, `DecidedAt`, `DecisionNotes`, and — the important one — a **snapshot of the prior values** so the Admin can revert if rejected.
- **Admin-side UI** to view and act on the queue. Per your earlier rule "Admin has no business whatsoever in the system other than user management, business intelligence, and approvals for manager changes," the Admin's Approvals tab becomes the home for this queue.

**Snapshot shape — the first decision.**

When the Manager edits a customer, we need to remember what the record looked like *before*. Three options:

- **(a)** Column-by-column. Add `PrevFirstName`, `PrevLastName`, `PrevContactNumber`, `PrevEmail`, `PrevBirthday`, `PrevPointsBalance`, etc. to the review row. Explicit, easy to query, but rigid — adding a customer field means adding a column here too.
- **(b)** JSON blob. One `SnapshotJson` text column holding the serialized previous values. Flexible — add customer fields without touching the review schema. But the values aren't queryable, and the Admin UI has to deserialize.
- **(c)** A soft-copy of the full customer row. Basically (a) with more columns.

My lean: **(b) JSON blob**. Reasons:

1. The snapshot is opaque to the system — nobody queries it, it's just read back out when the Admin reverts.
2. Customer fields will grow.
3. EF Core 8+/9 has first-class `ToJson()` for owned types, which is clean. Or just `string SnapshotJson` with manual serialize/deserialize if you'd rather not use `ToJson()`.

If you prefer **(a)**, the columns are trivial, it's just a wider table.

**Second decision — what triggers the review row.**

Two options:

- **(a)** Only Manager edits trigger a review. Admin edits don't (Admin *is* the approver). But the API's `UpdateCustomer` doesn't know who's editing — it takes a `UpdateCustomerDto` with no actor field. **We'd need to add `EditedBy` to the DTO or read the JWT claim.** Reading the JWT is cleaner; we already do that in `EmployeesController` and just added it to `CustomerController` for the `CreateCustomer` role check.
- **(b)** All edits trigger a review, and Admin edits just auto-approve themselves (weird, but simple).

My lean: **(a)**. Read the caller's employee ID and role from the JWT. If role is Manager, write a review row. If role is Admin, don't.

**Third decision — what does "revert" mean?**

If the Admin rejects a Manager's edit, what happens?

- **(a)** The customer row goes back to exactly the snapshot values (name, contact, email, birthday — the fields the Manager could have changed). Points balance and LastVisitDate aren't editable through the edit form, so they're untouched.
- **(b)** Only the fields that differ between snapshot and current get reverted.
- **(c)** Some other semantic.

My lean: **(a)**. Simple: "reject = roll the row back to how it was before the edit." Since the edit form can only touch five fields (name, contact, email, birthday — per M1's spec), that's all the snapshot needs to hold.

**Fourth decision — can the Manager edit again while a review is pending?**

Suppose the Manager edits a customer's phone number, that goes to the review queue as Pending. Before the Admin acts on it, the Manager edits the same customer again (changes the email this time). What happens?

- **(a)** Second edit supersedes the first: the old pending review row is discarded and a new one captures the state before *the first* edit. Rejecting the second edit rolls back to before the first.
- **(b)** Both edits queue separately. Admin sees two pending reviews for the same customer; rejecting the second rolls back only the second edit's fields.
- **(c)** Second edit is blocked until the first is resolved.

My lean: **(a)**. One pending review per customer at a time, always capturing "the last known-good state." Simpler to reason about; matches "revert" semantics.

**Fifth decision — where does the Admin see the queue?**

Your Admin nav currently has Dashboard, Approvals, Manage Users. The Approvals tab is a placeholder. It becomes real now, with at least the customer-edit-review section. Two shapes:

- **(a)** One Approvals tab with a **grid of pending customer-edit reviews**, click a row to open a drawer showing "before vs. after" side by side, and Approve / Reject buttons.
- **(b)** Same as (a), but also a second section for campaign-creation reviews (when M4b lands).

Since M4b is next after M4, I'd design the Approvals tab with **two sections from the start** — "Customer Edits" and "Campaign Creations" — even though Campaign Creations is empty until M4b. Or wait and only build Customer Edits now, and add the second section when M4b lands.

My lean: **build only Customer Edits now**. Add Campaign Creations as a second section in M4b. Keeps each chunk self-contained.

**Sixth decision — how do the before/after values get shown?**

The Admin wants to see what changed. Options:

- **(a)** Side-by-side: two columns, "Before" and "After," one row per field. Shows the delta clearly.
- **(b)** Inline highlighting: single column, changed fields marked. Harder to build cleanly in WinForms.
- **(c)** Just dump both rows: "Before: {...} / After: {...}." Ugly but simple.

My lean: **(a)**. Two-column table in the drawer.

**Seventh decision — what happens on approve?**

Just flips the review row's status to `Approved`. No change to the customer record (the edit already applied). One field update, done.

**Eighth decision — what happens on reject?**

Revert the customer to the snapshot values, then flip the review row's status to `Reverted`, record `DecidedBy`, `DecidedAt`, `DecisionNotes` (rejection reason — required, per the pattern we've established).

**One more — do we record a `DecisionNotes` on approve?**

Optional, same as everywhere else. Required on reject.

## What I need from you before M4 goes out

Short answers, or "defaults are fine":

1. **Snapshot shape:** JSON blob (b) or column-by-column (a)?
2. **Trigger:** only Manager edits write a review row; Admin edits don't. Confirm.
3. **Revert semantic:** full rollback to snapshot (a). Confirm.
4. **Concurrent edits:** second pending edit supersedes first (a). Confirm.
5. **Approvals tab scope:** Customer Edits only for M4; add Campaign Creations in M4b. Confirm.
6. **Before/after display:** side-by-side table (a). Confirm.
7. **Reject reason required, approve notes optional.** Confirm.

Once those are answered, I'll lay out M4 as a numbered list of sub-steps and we go one at a time.

```csharp
        private async void DeactivateCustomerBtn_Click(object? sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            if (_selectedCustomer is null) return;

            var customer = _selectedCustomer;

            var confirm = MessageBox.Show(
                FindForm(),
                $"Deactivate {customer.FullName}? They will no longer appear in the grid, " +
                $"but their order history and {customer.PointsBalance:N0} points are preserved.",
                "Deactivate Customer",
                MessageBoxButtons.YesNo,
                MessageBoxIcon.Warning);

            if (confirm != DialogResult.Yes) return;

            try
            {
                _deactivateCustomerBtn.Enabled = false;

                await _controller.DeactivateCustomerAsync(customer.CustomerId);

                Toast.Show(this, $"Deactivated {customer.FullName}.", ToastKind.Success);

                // Clear selection and reload — the customer won't appear in the grid
                // anymore (the API filters IsActive = false out of the list).
                _selectedCustomer = null;
                await ReloadCustomersAsync();
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                MessageBox.Show(FindForm(), ex.Message, "Deactivate failed");
            }
            finally
            {
                _deactivateCustomerBtn.Enabled = true;
            }
        }
```

Note the trailing blank line so the following method stays cleanly separated.

**回答：**

Got it, four changes. Let me restate them so we're aligned, then do them one at a time as usual.

**1. Customer deactivate works like Admin's user management.** The customer isn't hidden — it stays in the grid, muted, and the default filter just excludes inactive ones. A filter dropdown (like the status filter on Feedback) lets you flip the view to "show inactive" or "show all." So:

- `CustomerManagementView` gets a filter dropdown: **Active** (default) / **Inactive** / **All**.
- API `GetCustomers` gains an `activeFilter` param — currently it hard-filters `IsActive`, so `All` and `Inactive` return nothing.
- Inactive rows render muted (greyed text + muted background), same pattern as `ManageUsersView`'s inactive rows.
- Deactivating a customer doesn't clear the selection — the row just mutes in place.

**2. Admin's user management disabled-state is too subtle.** Currently when a Manager tries to act on an Admin's row, `editBtn.Enabled = false` etc., but WinForms's `ButtonStyler.TrackEnabledState` fades to `ButtonDisabledFill` / `ButtonDisabledText`, which reads as "1% faded." You want it to read as **50% — clearly off.** So: adjust the disabled palette so disabled buttons look genuinely disabled (muted fill, muted text, visually distinct). This affects `ButtonStyler` globally, since the same disabled style is used in every view. That's the correct place to fix it.

**3. Same disabled treatment for Customer side.** When a Manager opens a customer with deactivate disabled (or any button that's `Enabled = false`), it should look 50% off, not 1% off. This falls out of fix #2 automatically if we change the palette — no per-view work needed.

**4. Campaign edit modal contrast is bad.** When the modal switches to edit mode, the form panel background is currently `SurfacePrimary` (white) with input fields on it — but you're saying the *modal's* background and the panel don't read well. You want:

- Modal background → pure white.
- Form/edit panel → brand color (or brand-tinted).

Let me look at what the modal does today. From `FrmCampaignDetail.BuildLayout`:

- Form `BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary` (which is `White`).
- `_formPanel` has no explicit `BackColor` — it inherits from the form.
- `_viewPanel` has `BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfaceCard`.

So the form is already white. If it feels off, it's probably because the **view panel** uses `SurfaceCard` (a tan tint) and the **form panel** is white — inconsistent. You want the form/edit mode to have the brand color as the panel, and the modal chrome to be pure white.

Concretely:

- Form-level `BackColor` stays `SurfacePrimary` (white).
- `_formPanel` gets an explicit `BackColor = BrandPalette.Brand`? That would be very dark — all text on it would need to be light. That doesn't match the brand's neutral-content philosophy.
- **Or** `_formPanel` gets `SurfaceCard` (the same tan as the view panel), so both modes look consistent — the whole content area is tan, the modal chrome is white. I think this is what you actually want: consistency between view and edit.

**Confirm which reading #4 is:**

- **(a)** Both panels tan (`SurfaceCard`), chrome white — consistent look between view and edit.
- **(b)** Form panel gets actual brand color (`Brand` — dark brown), which would require inverted text colors.
- **(c)** Something else.

My lean: **(a)**.

That's what I should have said earlier. Here's the corrected fix.

## Fix — solid chrome strip between panel and buttons

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein/Views/Forms/FrmCampaignDetail.cs`

**Search for** (in `BuildLayout`):

```csharp
            _errorLabel = new Label
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Bottom,
                Height = 26,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(8.5f),
                ForeColor = BrandPalette.StatusNegativeFill,
                TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleLeft,
                BackColor = Color.Transparent,
            };
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            _errorLabel = new Label
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Bottom,
                Height = 26,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(8.5f),
                ForeColor = BrandPalette.StatusNegativeFill,
                TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleLeft,
                // Solid chrome color, not transparent. This label sits between the white
                // content panel and the action row; a transparent background let the
                // panel extend underneath with no visible gap. An opaque strip here is
                // what creates the visual separation.
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfaceCard,
                Padding = new Padding(18, 0, 0, 0),   // align with the panel's left inset
            };
```

**But this creates a new problem.** The content panel (`_viewPanel` / `_formPanel`, `Dock.Fill`) is added **after** the error label in the `Controls.Add` sequence. Higher z-order goes on top. So the panel would paint **over** the error label's tan strip, and we're back to the panel touching the buttons.

**Fix for that:** change the `Controls.Add` order so the error label and action row are added *after* the content panels. That puts them at higher z-order, on top of the panel.

**Search for:**

```csharp
            // Compose. Dock order matters — added bottom-to-top visually.
            Controls.Add(_actionRow);
            Controls.Add(_errorLabel);
            Controls.Add(_formPanel);
            Controls.Add(_viewPanel);
            Controls.Add(subtitleLabel);
            Controls.Add(titleLabel);
            PositionActionButtons(_actionRow);
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // Compose. The Fill panels go in first so they have the LOWEST z-order in
            // their dock band; the error label and action row go in after so they paint
            // on top of the panel's bottom edge. This is what gives the panel a clean cut
            // with a visible tan strip above the buttons, instead of the panel extending
            // underneath them.
            Controls.Add(_viewPanel);
            Controls.Add(_formPanel);
            Controls.Add(_errorLabel);
            Controls.Add(_actionRow);
            Controls.Add(subtitleLabel);
            Controls.Add(titleLabel);
            PositionActionButtons(_actionRow);
```

**Dock order caveat.** In WinForms, docking is resolved by z-order too — the control that's docked first (highest z-order) claims its edge first, and later ones fit around it. Since both Fill panels and the Bottom-docked panels need to occupy distinct regions, changing the add order affects which docked controls "win" the space. Let me think:

- `_viewPanel` / `_formPanel`: `Dock.Fill`. Fills whatever space remains.
- `_errorLabel` / `_actionRow`: `Dock.Bottom`. Claim strips at the bottom.
- `subtitleLabel` / `titleLabel`: `Dock.Top`. Claim strips at the top.

WinForms resolves docking in z-order from **highest to lowest**, and higher-z controls claim their edge first. The control added last has the **highest z-order** (since `Controls.Add` puts new controls at index 0, which is the top of z-order). So:

- With the new order, `titleLabel` is added last → highest z → claims top first.
- `subtitleLabel` → next.
- `_actionRow` → claims bottom next.
- `_errorLabel` → claims its bottom strip next.
- `_formPanel` / `_viewPanel` → Fill, gets what's left.

That's the *correct* order. With the original order (`_actionRow` added first → lowest z → claims edge last), WinForms was resolving Fill first, then Bottom, and the Fill panel ended up covering the error label's strip. Which is exactly the "no gap" symptom you saw.

So the reorder fixes it. Good.

You already said you wanted the modal taller. Bump it.

```csharp
                Visible = false,

```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
                Visible = false,
            };
```

With the reordering fix from above, the border should now be visible on all four sides — the bottom edge will sit at the top of the tan strip that the error label paints, and nothing will clip it.

## Summary of edits

1. `_errorLabel`: `BackColor = Color.Transparent` → `BrandPalette.SurfaceCard`, with a small left `Padding`.
2. `Controls.Add` order in `BuildLayout`: content panels first, then error label, then action row, then subtitle, then title. (This is the actual fix for the "squished / no gap" issue.)
3. `ClientSize`: `600, 640` → `600, 720`.
4. `_viewPanel`: put the `BorderStyle = BorderStyle.FixedSingle` back.

**回答：**

Fix #4 is done. On to fix #2 — the global disabled-button palette.

This is the one that makes disabled buttons actually read as disabled, app-wide, and by extension fixes #3 (the Customer-side disabled states) since they use the same `ButtonStyler.TrackEnabledState`.

## Where the change goes

Two files:

- **`BrandPalette.cs`** — the disabled fill/text tokens are the actual colors. Currently:
  ```csharp
  public static Color ButtonDisabledFill => Tone80;
  public static Color ButtonDisabledText => Tone35;
  ```
  `Tone80` is a light neutral grey. `Tone35` is a mid-grey. Both are pale, which is why the fade reads as "1% off." The fix is darker fill, lighter text, so disabled actually reads as off.
- **`ButtonStyler.cs`** — the mechanism is fine; the swap between active and disabled colors happens on `EnabledChanged`. Only one thing to check: `FlatStyle.Flat` buttons don't repaint their fill on `Enabled` flips, which `ButtonStyler` already handles by explicitly setting `BackColor` / `ForeColor`. So no change needed here.

So the fix is **only in `BrandPalette.cs`**.

## The patch

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein/Theme/BrandPalette.cs`

**Search for:**

```csharp
        // Plain neutral grey — deliberately NOT a tint/shade of the brand color, so a
        // disabled button reads as "off" rather than as a duller version of the same action.
        public static Color ButtonDisabledFill => Tone80;
        public static Color ButtonDisabledText => Tone35;
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
        // Disabled state — deliberately a strong, low-contrast-to-active grey pair so a
        // disabled button reads clearly as "off" rather than as a duller version of the
        // same action. Earlier values (Tone80 fill, Tone35 text) were both pale enough
        // that a disabled button looked almost identical to an enabled secondary button.
        // Now: darker fill + lighter text, well separated from every active palette entry.
        public static Color ButtonDisabledFill => Tone35;
        public static Color ButtonDisabledText => Tint90;
```

Two token swaps:

- **`ButtonDisabledFill`**: `Tone80` → `Tone35`. `Tone35` is a much darker neutral grey — closer to mid-grey, clearly not a light active-state tint.
- **`ButtonDisabledText`**: `Tone35` → `Tint90`. `Tint90` is a near-white tan. High contrast against the darker fill.

The net effect: disabled buttons become dark grey with light text, instead of light grey with mid-grey text.

## What else uses those tokens

Search the codebase for `ButtonDisabledFill` and `ButtonDisabledText`. It's set only in `ButtonStyler.cs`, which every view already routes through. So this is a **one-place change** — every disabled button across the app updates at once:

- Manage Users: Edit / Reset Password / Deactivate (on an Admin row) — now clearly dark and off.
- Customers: Edit Customer / Deactivate Customer (when a Barista somehow lands there — shouldn't happen, but the gate uses `Enabled`) — same treatment.
- TransactionView: the Log Sale button when the cart is empty.
- Everywhere else that uses `ButtonStyler.TrackEnabledState`.

## Rebuild and check

1. Log in as Admin → Manage Users.
2. Select an Admin row (Kyle Bautista in your seed). The three buttons — Edit Details, Reset Password, Deactivate Employee — should now be **dark grey with light text**, unmistakably disabled.
3. Select a Barista row. The same three buttons should be **light tan / brand**, unmistakably enabled.
4. Click into the Customers tab as Manager — the Edit/Deactivate Customer buttons should be normal. If you were to log in as a Barista (who can't see them), no change. So no visible change on the customer side from this patch alone — it just ensures consistency if the disabled path ever triggers.

**One thing to watch:** in some views the disabled buttons might now stand out *more* than the enabled ones because they're darker. If that reads wrong (e.g. the disabled Log Sale button draws more attention than the enabled version would), tell me and I'll adjust to a mid-grey that's clearly off without being louder than active. But I think `Tone35` fill with `Tint90` text lands in the right spot.

Rebuild and take a screenshot of Manage Users with an Admin row selected. If the disabled state reads correctly, we move to fix #1 (customer filter + inactive rendering + API param).

**提问：**

the problem is that the tones itself is kind of bad, theyre themed and i would want it to be visually grey. here are the differences of swapping, first two images is default (first disabled, second enabled), the next few is the change.

---

**回答：**

You're right, and the screenshots make it clear. What I gave you is a **warmer, darker tan** on both states — not grey. The disabled looks almost the same as enabled except slightly darker, which is exactly the problem we were trying to solve. And "grey" in your complaint means **actually neutral grey**, not a brand-tinted tone.

## Why it looks that way

Both `Tone80` and `Tone35` are derived from the **brand color** by the `Tone()` function:

```csharp
private static Color Tone(Color c, double amount)
{
    var grey = Mix(c, Color.Black, 0.5);
    grey = Mix(grey, Color.White, 0.5);
    return Mix(c, grey, amount);
}
```

`Tone()` mixes toward a "grey" that is itself derived from the brand — so every "tone" is a warm brownish-grey. That's by design in this palette — every color in the app is a tint/tone/shade of brand brown, nothing is truly neutral. But for **disabled states specifically**, you want the universal "greyed out" affordance, which is a neutral hue that doesn't compete with any brand color.

## The fix

Define two genuinely neutral greys, separate from the brand-mixing functions. Add them to `BrandPalette` as raw RGB values.

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein/Theme/BrandPalette.cs`

**Search for:**

```csharp
        // Disabled state — deliberately a strong, low-contrast-to-active grey pair so a
        // disabled button reads clearly as "off" rather than as a duller version of the
        // same action. Earlier values (Tone80 fill, Tone35 text) were both pale enough
        // that a disabled button looked almost identical to an enabled secondary button.
        // Now: darker fill + lighter text, well separated from every active palette entry.
        public static Color ButtonDisabledFill => Tone35;
        public static Color ButtonDisabledText => Tint90;
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
        // Disabled state — genuinely NEUTRAL greys, deliberately NOT derived from the
        // brand color. Every other color in this palette is a tint/tone/shade of the brand
        // brown, which is correct for active UI. But "disabled" is a universal affordance
        // that reads most clearly as a plain hue-neutral grey — a brand-tinted "disabled"
        // button looks like a different active state, not an off state.
        //
        // These are raw RGB values, not passed through Tone()/Tint()/Shade().
        public static Color ButtonDisabledFill => Color.FromArgb(255, 200, 200, 200);
        public static Color ButtonDisabledText => Color.FromArgb(255, 120, 120, 120);
```

Two truly neutral greys:

- **Fill:** `RGB(200, 200, 200)` — a standard light-medium grey. Same channel value across R/G/B, so no warm or cool cast.
- **Text:** `RGB(120, 120, 120)` — a mid-grey. High enough contrast against the fill to be readable, low enough contrast against the surrounding whites to read as "muted / off."

## What this does

- Disabled buttons everywhere become neutral grey — unmistakably "off," not "a darker tan."
- Enabled buttons keep their existing look (tan secondary fill, brand brown primary fill).
- The two states are now visually unambiguous: warm tan = available; neutral grey = disabled.

## One consideration

This is a deliberate, small break from the palette's "every color is a brand tint" rule. Every other token in `BrandPalette` is warm. Adding two cool-grey values is a targeted exception just for the disabled affordance, and it's the standard pattern in brand-heavy UI systems (the disabled state is often the one place a strict brand palette makes an exception, because "greyed out" is a strong universal signal).

If you want it *even* more obviously disabled, we can go further:

- **Fill:** `RGB(180, 180, 180)` — a step darker.
- **Text:** `RGB(100, 100, 100)` — a step darker, less readable, more clearly "off."

But try the `200 / 120` pair first. It's the standard WinForms-era disabled look.

## Rebuild and check

Log in as Admin → Manage Users → select an Admin row. The three buttons should now be **neutral grey fill with mid-grey text** — unambiguously disabled. Select a Barista row. The three buttons should be normal tan. The difference should be obvious at a glance.

Take a screenshot of both states side by side. If the disabled still doesn't read right, tell me which direction (lighter, darker, more contrast with the text) and I'll tune the two RGB values.

**回答：**

Two things:

1. **The change didn't take effect** — you rebuilt but the buttons look the same. That means the old values are still being used somewhere, or `ButtonStyler.TrackEnabledState` isn't actually driving those particular buttons. I'll address that below.
2. **You want a warmer grey**, not neutral. That's a middle ground — a grey that reads as "off" but with a slight warm cast so it doesn't look foreign next to the tan palette.

Let me solve both.

## Fix A — warmer grey disabled colors

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein/Theme/BrandPalette.cs`

**Search for:**

```csharp
        // Disabled state — genuinely NEUTRAL greys, deliberately NOT derived from the
        // brand color. Every other color in this palette is a tint/tone/shade of the brand
        // brown, which is correct for active UI. But "disabled" is a universal affordance
        // that reads most clearly as a plain hue-neutral grey — a brand-tinted "disabled"
        // button looks like a different active state, not an off state.
        //
        // These are raw RGB values, not passed through Tone()/Tint()/Shade().
        public static Color ButtonDisabledFill => Color.FromArgb(255, 200, 200, 200);
        public static Color ButtonDisabledText => Color.FromArgb(255, 120, 120, 120);
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
        // Disabled state — warm neutral grey. Not brand-tinted (that reads as a "darker
        // active state"), but not cool-neutral either (that reads as foreign against the
        // warm tan palette). The channels are slightly skewed toward red/yellow so the
        // grey sits alongside the tan without clashing:
        //
        //   Fill: RGB(210, 205, 198)  — R > G > B by a few points, warm cast
        //   Text: RGB(135, 128, 120)  — same skew, darker, readable on the fill
        //
        // Both are explicit raw RGB values, not passed through Tone()/Tint()/Shade().
        public static Color ButtonDisabledFill => Color.FromArgb(255, 210, 205, 198);
        public static Color ButtonDisabledText => Color.FromArgb(255, 135, 128, 120);
```

RGB values explained:

- **`210, 205, 198`** — R is highest, then G, then B. That's a warm cast (browns and tans have more red than blue). Compared to pure grey `200, 200, 200`, this shifts toward the palette's warmth without inheriting the brand color's saturation.
- **`135, 128, 120`** — same skew, darker. Reads as muted text on the fill, clearly lower contrast than active text.

## Fix B — why the change didn't take

**`ButtonStyler.TrackEnabledState` captures the button's colors at the moment it's called.**

```csharp
public static void TrackEnabledState(Button button)
{
    var activeBackColor = button.BackColor;
    var activeForeColor = button.ForeColor;

    void Apply()
    {
        button.BackColor = button.Enabled ? activeBackColor : BrandPalette.ButtonDisabledFill;
        button.ForeColor = button.Enabled ? activeForeColor : BrandPalette.ButtonDisabledText;
    }

    button.EnabledChanged += (s, e) => Apply();
    Apply();
}
```

The `Apply()` function **captures `activeBackColor`/`activeForeColor` once**, at hook-up time. Then whenever `Enabled` changes, it swaps between the captured active colors and the current `ButtonDisabledFill`/`ButtonDisabledText`.

So the disabled colors *should* update when you rebuild — because `Apply()` reads `BrandPalette.ButtonDisabledFill` at call time, and you rebuilt with new values.

**Unless `Apply()` was never called for those buttons.** Two scenarios:

- **Scenario 1:** `TrackEnabledState` was never called on the Edit/Reset/Deactivate buttons in `ManageUsersView`. Short answer: **no, one reference each is correct.**

`ButtonDisabledFill` and `ButtonDisabledText` are read in exactly one place — inside `ButtonStyler.TrackEnabledState`'s `Apply()` local function. Every button in the app that goes through `TrackEnabledState` uses those same two properties, but the **read happens in one method**, so VS's "Find All References" shows **1 reference** each. That's the shape you want.

Contrast with something like `ButtonPrimaryFill`, which gets referenced from every view that creates a primary button (Login, Transaction, Customers, Feedback, Manage Users, Campaigns, modals...) — it'd have 10+ references. Fix #1a — API-side filter on `GetCustomers`.

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein.api/Controllers/CustomerController.cs`

**Search for:**

```csharp
        [HttpGet]
        public async Task<ActionResult<PagedResponse<CustomerResponseDto>>> GetCustomers(
            int companyId,
            [FromQuery] string? search,
            [FromQuery] int page = 1,
            [FromQuery] int pageSize = 25)
        {
            if (page < 1) page = 1;
            if (pageSize < 1) pageSize = 25;
            if (pageSize > 200) pageSize = 200;

            await using var tenant = await _tenantFactory.CreateAsync(companyId);

            var query = tenant.Customers
                .AsNoTracking()
                .Where(c => c.IsActive);
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
        [HttpGet]
        public async Task<ActionResult<PagedResponse<CustomerResponseDto>>> GetCustomers(
            int companyId,
            [FromQuery] string? search,
            [FromQuery] string? activeFilter = null,
            [FromQuery] int page = 1,
            [FromQuery] int pageSize = 25)
        {
            if (page < 1) page = 1;
            if (pageSize < 1) pageSize = 25;
            if (pageSize > 200) pageSize = 200;

            await using var tenant = await _tenantFactory.CreateAsync(companyId);

            // activeFilter:
            //   null / "" / "active"    -> only IsActive = true (the default)
            //   "inactive"              -> only IsActive = false
            //   "all"                   -> no IsActive filter
            // Anything else falls back to the default (active-only).
            var filter = (activeFilter ?? string.Empty).Trim().ToLowerInvariant();

            var query = tenant.Customers.AsNoTracking();

            query = filter switch
            {
                "inactive" => query.Where(c => !c.IsActive),
                "all"      => query,
                _          => query.Where(c => c.IsActive),
            };
```

**What this does:**

- Adds `activeFilter` as a query parameter, positioned between `search` and `page`. It's optional — callers that don't send it get the existing behavior (active only).
- The three branches: `inactive` returns only deactivated, `all` returns everything, anything else (including missing) returns active only.
- The old `.Where(c => c.IsActive)` that was baked into the query declaration is moved into the `switch` — so the base query is now unfiltered and the switch decides.

**What it does NOT touch:** the `search` clause, the projection, pagination, or any other endpoint in this controller. The other methods (`GetCustomer`, `FindCustomer`, `UpdateCustomer`, `DeleteCustomer`, `GetLedger`, `GetOrderHistory`) are unchanged.

**Important compatibility note:** because `activeFilter` is placed *before* `page` in the signature, any existing caller that passes positional arguments — `GetCustomers(companyId, search, 1, 25)` — would now bind `1` to `activeFilter` and `25` to `page`. **Check `CustomerApi.GetCustomersAsync` on the WinForms side** — it builds a URL with `?page=...&pageSize=...&search=...`, so it uses named query params, not positional arguments. No breakage there. But if you have any other caller passing positional args, tell me and I'll reorder.

Rebuild, and you can smoke-test with curl if you want:

- `GET /api/tenant/1/customers?page=1&pageSize=25` — active only (existing behavior).
- `GET /api/tenant/1/customers?activeFilter=inactive&page=1&pageSize=25` — deactivated only.
- `GET /api/tenant/1/customers?activeFilter=all&page=1&pageSize=25` — everything.

`[Authorize]` on the controller means you need a Bearer token. Once the build passes, prompt me for 1b (WinForms `CustomerApi` + `CustomerController` passthrough).

```csharp
        public async Task<PagedResponse<CustomerResponseDto>> GetCustomersAsync(
            string? search = null, int page = 1, int pageSize = 25)
                {
                    var url = $"api/tenant/{ApiConfig.CompanyId}/customers?page={page}&pageSize={pageSize}";
                    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(search))
                        url += $"&search={Uri.EscapeDataString(search)}";

                    var response = await _http.GetAsync(url);
                    await EnsureSuccess(response);

                    var result = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<PagedResponse<CustomerResponseDto>>();
                    return result ?? new PagedResponse<CustomerResponseDto>();
                }
```

```csharp
        public async Task<PagedResponse<CustomerResponseDto>> GetCustomersAsync(
            string? search = null, int page = 1, int pageSize = 25, string? activeFilter = null)
        {
            var url = $"api/tenant/{ApiConfig.CompanyId}/customers?page={page}&pageSize={pageSize}";
            if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(search))
                url += $"&search={Uri.EscapeDataString(search)}";
            if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(activeFilter))
                url += $"&activeFilter={Uri.EscapeDataString(activeFilter)}";

            var response = await _http.GetAsync(url);
            await EnsureSuccess(response);

            var result = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<PagedResponse<CustomerResponseDto>>();
            return result ?? new PagedResponse<CustomerResponseDto>();
        }
```

```csharp
        /// <summary>
        /// Builds the "Filter by Status:" row and inserts it into the card header, below
        /// the search box. Same shape as the Feedback status filter: label, then dropdown,
        /// positions computed from the label's measured width. Default is Active.
        ///
        /// The card header was 60px tall for search + button; this needs another ~40px
        /// below the search row, so the header grows.
        /// </summary>
        private void BuildActiveFilterRow()
        {
            // Grow the header so the new row fits below the search box.
            // Search box lives at y=16..44; filter row starts at y=52.
            cardHeaderPanel.Height = 92;

            _activeFilterRow = new Panel
            {
                Location = new Point(16, 52),
                Size = new Size(360, 30),
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
            };

            var label = new Label
            {
                Text = "Filter by Status:",
                AutoSize = true,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(9.5f),
                ForeColor = BrandPalette.NeutralTextMuted,
                BackColor = Color.Transparent,
            };

            _activeFilterCombo = new ComboBox
            {
                Size = new Size(180, 26),
                DropDownStyle = ComboBoxStyle.DropDownList,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(9.5f),
            };

            _activeFilterCombo.Items.Add(ActiveFilterActiveOption);
            _activeFilterCombo.Items.Add(ActiveFilterInactiveOption);
            _activeFilterCombo.Items.Add(ActiveFilterAllOption);

            // Default to Active — matches the API's default and keeps Baristas from ever
            // seeing deactivated customers.
            _activeFilterCombo.SelectedItem = ActiveFilterActiveOption;

            // Position: label first, combo after, measured so they can't collide.
            var labelWidth = TextRenderer.MeasureText(label.Text, label.Font).Width;
            label.Left = 0;
            label.Top = (30 - label.Height) / 2;

            _activeFilterCombo.Left = labelWidth + 12;
            _activeFilterCombo.Top = (30 - _activeFilterCombo.Height) / 2;

            _activeFilterCombo.SelectedIndexChanged += async (s, e) =>
            {
                // Filter change is always a fresh page-1 query — same as a search change.
                await ReloadCustomersAsync();
            };

            _activeFilterRow.Controls.Add(_activeFilterCombo);
            _activeFilterRow.Controls.Add(label);

            cardHeaderPanel.Controls.Add(_activeFilterRow);
            _activeFilterRow.BringToFront();
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// The API value for the currently-selected filter:
        ///   "Active"   -> "active"
        ///   "Inactive" -> "inactive"
        ///   "All"      -> "all"
        /// Null (never happens with the fixed list, but defensive) -> "active".
        /// </summary>
        private string SelectedActiveFilter =>
            _activeFilterCombo?.SelectedItem as string switch
            {
                ActiveFilterInactiveOption => "inactive",
                ActiveFilterAllOption => "all",
                _ => "active",
            };
```

Build passed. One new warning worth fixing — `CS8848` on line 191.

## The warning

```text
CustomerManagementView.cs(191,56,191,62): warning CS8848: Operator 'switch' cannot be used here due to precedence. Use parentheses to disambiguate.
```

That's in `SelectedActiveFilter`. I wrote:

```csharp
private string SelectedActiveFilter =>
    _activeFilterCombo?.SelectedItem as string switch
    {
        ActiveFilterInactiveOption => "inactive",
        ActiveFilterAllOption => "all",
        _ => "active",
    };
```

The compiler parses `_activeFilterCombo?.SelectedItem as string switch { ... }` as `_activeFilterCombo?.SelectedItem as (string switch { ... })` — the `as` binds tighter than `switch`, so it complains. **It happens to still compile** because the pattern arms are string literals and it can make the types line up, but the warning is real and the behavior might not be what I intended.

The fix is parentheses.

**回答：**

Three things, and the third one is a real bug. Let me take them in order.

## 1. The disabled-state bug — "it still says Deactivate even if it's deactivated"

Looking at `RefreshDrawerAsync` in `CustomerManagementView`, there's no logic that changes `_deactivateCustomerBtn`'s text or state based on the customer's `IsActive`. The button is always labeled "Deactivate Customer" and always enabled (for Managers).

Two things wrong with that:

- If the customer is already inactive, the button should say **"Reactivate Customer"** (or at least be hidden/disabled).
- The API's `DELETE /customers/{id}` only sets `IsActive = false`. There's **no reactivate endpoint** — so even if we relabel the button, clicking it would do nothing new. Reactivation would require a new API method.

So this is actually a two-part fix:

- **(a)** Add `POST /customers/{id}/reactivate` to the API.
- **(b)** In `RefreshDrawerAsync`, look at `customer.IsActive` and swap the button's text between "Deactivate Customer" and "Reactivate Customer."

**Before I write that** — do you want reactivation to be possible from this drawer? Or should an inactive customer just be visible-but-not-actionable (i.e. the button hides entirely when the customer is already deactivated)?

My lean: **add reactivation.** It's the same shape as the employee reactivate endpoint that already exists in `EmployeesController`, it's a five-minute API addition, and a Manager who deactivates a customer by mistake has a real need to undo it. But it's your call — you might prefer "inactive is a one-way door; contact admin."

**Question 1:** reactivate button (yes/no), or hide the button when already inactive?

## 2. Primary vs. secondary button distinction

You want a clear visual hierarchy: **primary = filled brand brown**, **secondary = outlined / no fill**. Right now a lot of buttons use `ButtonSecondaryFill` (light tan fill), which reads as "soft primary" — not clearly secondary.

Standard convention:

- **Primary** (the one action that confirms / saves / commits): filled brand brown, white text.
- **Secondary** (cancel, close, alternate actions): transparent or white background, brand text, **1px brand-colored border**, no fill.
- **Destructive** (deactivate, reject): same as secondary, but with a red-ish or status-negative text color. Or a special "destructive primary" style.

Let me add two new palette entries for the outlined secondary, then patch the buttons that should use them.

**Palette additions:**

```csharp
public static Color ButtonSecondaryFill_Outlined => Color.Transparent;
public static Color ButtonSecondaryBorder => BrandPalette.Brand;
public static Color ButtonSecondaryText_Outlined => BrandPalette.Brand;
```

Actually, cleaner to add just two things:

```csharp
// Outlined secondary — no fill, brand border, brand text. Use for Cancel, Close,
// and alternate actions where the soft-tan ButtonSecondaryFill reads too "primary."
public static Color ButtonOutlinedFill => Color.Transparent;
public static Color ButtonOutlinedBorder => BrandPalette.Brand;
public static Color ButtonOutlinedText => BrandPalette.Brand;
```

And a small helper in `ButtonStyler` to apply the outlined look:

```csharp
public static void ApplyOutlined(Button button)
{
    button.FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat;
    button.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 1;
    button.FlatAppearance.BorderColor = BrandPalette.ButtonOutlinedBorder;
    button.BackColor = BrandPalette.ButtonOutlinedFill;
    button.ForeColor = BrandPalette.ButtonOutlinedText;
}
```

**Where to apply outlined style:**

The button families that should switch from "soft tan fill" to "outlined":

- `FrmCampaignDetail`: `_closeBtn`, `_cancelBtn` → outlined. `_editBtn` → outlined. `_deactivateBtn` → outlined with status-negative text. `_activateBtn` → outlined. `_primaryBtn` stays filled (it's the confirm action).
- `ManageUsersView`: `editBtn`, `resetPasswordBtn` → outlined. `deactivateBtn` → outlined with status-negative text. (`deactivateBtn` in this view already had negative text; the fill stays tan for now.)
- `CustomerManagementView`: `_editCustomerBtn`, `_deactivateCustomerBtn` → outlined. `submitRequestBtn`, `approveBtn` stay filled. `rejectBtn` → outlined with status-negative text.
- `FeedbackManagementView`: `_cancelTicketBtn` → outlined. `_resolveBtn` stays filled.
- `TransactionView`: `_promoMenuBtn` → could go either way. It's a picker, not a confirm. Outlined.
- `FrmMain` nav buttons: leave as-is (they're a different family).
- `PaginationControl`: leave as-is (tiny, already neutral).

**That's a broad sweep.** I'd rather not do it blind. Let me propose:

- **Step A**: Add `ButtonOutlinedFill` / `ButtonOutlinedBorder` / `ButtonOutlinedText` to `BrandPalette`, and `ButtonStyler.ApplyOutlined(Button)`.
- **Step B**: Apply outlined to the buttons in one view at a time. Start with `FrmCampaignDetail` since you're looking at it now, then `CustomerManagementView`, then `ManageUsersView`, etc.

**Question 2:** does that approach work, or do you want a different visual distinction than "1px brand-brown border + no fill"?

## 3. The screen with disabled customers

You confirmed 1a–1c work. The remaining item from the earlier list is **1d — mute inactive rows in the grid**. Not done yet. When the filter is set to Inactive or All, deactivated customers appear in the grid, and they should visually read as muted (greyed text + muted background), same as inactive employees in Manage Users.

**I'll do 1d in the same pass** as whatever answer you give for #1 and #2.

So the label flips based on state. Confirmed.

## The three patches

I'll do them in order: API endpoint first, then the label logic, then the muted-row rendering.

## Patch A — API: reactivate customer endpoint

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein.api/Controllers/CustomerController.cs`

**Search for** the closing of `DeleteCustomer`:

```csharp
        // DELETE api/tenant/{companyId}/customers/{id}
        // Soft delete — sets IsActive = false, does not remove the row. Preserves order history.
        [HttpDelete("{id:int}")]
        public async Task<IActionResult> DeleteCustomer(int companyId, int id)
        {
            await using var tenant = await _tenantFactory.CreateAsync(companyId);

            var customer = await tenant.Customers.FirstOrDefaultAsync(c => c.CustomerId == id);
            if (customer is null)
                return NotFound();

            customer.IsActive = false;
            customer.UpdatedAt = DateTime.UtcNow;

            try
            {
                await tenant.SaveChangesAsync();
            }
            catch (DbUpdateException ex)
            {
                return Conflict(new { message = ex.InnerException?.Message ?? ex.Message });
            }

            return NoContent();
        }
```

**Add immediately after that method's closing brace:**

```csharp
        // POST api/tenant/{companyId}/customers/{id}/reactivate
        // Reverses a soft delete — sets IsActive = true. All history preserved.
        [HttpPost("{id:int}/reactivate")]
        public async Task<IActionResult> ReactivateCustomer(int companyId, int id)
        {
            await using var tenant = await _tenantFactory.CreateAsync(companyId);

            var customer = await tenant.Customers.FirstOrDefaultAsync(c => c.CustomerId == id);
            if (customer is null)
                return NotFound();

            customer.IsActive = true;
            customer.UpdatedAt = DateTime.UtcNow;

            try
            {
                await tenant.SaveChangesAsync();
            }
            catch (DbUpdateException ex)
            {
                return Conflict(new { message = ex.InnerException?.Message ?? ex.Message });
            }

            return NoContent();
        }
```

**No role check.** The controller already has `[Authorize]` (from an earlier patch), and the UI gates the button to Managers. Adding an explicit role check here would be belt-and-suspenders; if you want it, say so and I'll add `CallerIsBarista`-style rejection. For now, any authenticated employee can call it, same as the existing `DeleteCustomer` endpoint.

**Test with curl after building:**

- `POST /api/tenant/1/customers/{id}/reactivate` with a Bearer token → `204 No Content`.
- The customer's `IsActive` flips to true in the DB.

```csharp
        private async void DeactivateCustomerBtn_Click(object? sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            if (_selectedCustomer is null) return;

            var customer = _selectedCustomer;

            var confirm = MessageBox.Show(
                FindForm(),
                $"Deactivate {customer.FullName}? They will no longer appear in the grid, " +
                $"but their order history and {customer.PointsBalance:N0} points are preserved.",
                "Deactivate Customer",
                MessageBoxButtons.YesNo,
                MessageBoxIcon.Warning);

            try
            {
                _deactivateCustomerBtn.Enabled = false;

                await _controller.DeactivateCustomerAsync(customer.CustomerId);

                Toast.Show(this, $"Deactivated {customer.FullName}.", ToastKind.Success);

                // Clear selection and reload — the customer won't appear in the grid
                // anymore (the API filters IsActive = false out of the list).
                _selectedCustomer = null;
                await ReloadCustomersAsync();
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                MessageBox.Show(FindForm(), ex.Message, "Deactivate failed");
            }
            finally
            {
                _deactivateCustomerBtn.Enabled = true;
            }

```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
        private async void DeactivateCustomerBtn_Click(object? sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            if (_selectedCustomer is null) return;

            var customer = _selectedCustomer;
            var reactivating = !customer.IsActive;

            var confirmMessage = reactivating
                ? $"Reactivate {customer.FullName}? They will reappear in the active customer list."
                : $"Deactivate {customer.FullName}? They will no longer appear in the grid, " +
                  $"but their order history and {customer.PointsBalance:N0} points are preserved.";

            var confirmTitle = reactivating ? "Reactivate Customer" : "Deactivate Customer";

            var confirm = MessageBox.Show(
                FindForm(),
                confirmMessage,
                confirmTitle,
                MessageBoxButtons.YesNo,
                MessageBoxIcon.Question);

            if (confirm != DialogResult.Yes) return;

            try
            {
                _deactivateCustomerBtn.Enabled = false;

                if (reactivating)
                {
                    await _controller.ReactivateCustomerAsync(customer.CustomerId);
                    Toast.Show(this, $"Reactivated {customer.FullName}.", ToastKind.Success);
                }
                else
                {
                    await _controller.DeactivateCustomerAsync(customer.CustomerId);
                    Toast.Show(this, $"Deactivated {customer.FullName}.", ToastKind.Success);
                }

                // Reload. If we're in the Active filter and just deactivated, the customer
                // drops out of the grid. If we're in the Inactive filter and just reactivated,
                // the same. If we're in All, the row stays but its state flips.
                await ReloadCustomersAsync();

                // Try to keep the customer selected if they're still visible under the
                // current filter. If they filtered themselves out, selection clears and the
                // drawer reverts to the empty state.
                SelectCustomerRowById(customer.CustomerId);
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                MessageBox.Show(FindForm(), ex.Message, "Operation failed");
            }
            finally
            {
                _deactivateCustomerBtn.Enabled = true;
            }
        }
```

**One nuance:** the previous version cleared `_selectedCustomer` before reloading. Now we keep the customer object and try to re-select them after the reload. If the reload dropped them from the grid (filter change), `SelectCustomerRowById` finds no matching row and silently leaves the drawer empty. That's the right behavior.

**回答：**

Good catch — that's a real gap. Right now when you select a deactivated employee in Manage Users, the drawer shows them normally and only the Edit/Reset/Deactivate buttons grey out. You want the whole profile to read as locked-down: no fields editable, no actions except Reactivate.

Let me look at what `RefreshDrawer` currently does. From the earlier code:

```csharp
var isAdminRow = emp.Role.Equals("Admin", ...) || emp.Role.Equals("SuperAdmin", ...);
editBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow;
resetPasswordBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow;
deactivateBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow;
deactivateBtn.Text = emp.IsActive ? "Deactivate Employee" : "Reactivate Employee";
deactivateBtn.ForeColor = emp.IsActive ? BrandPalette.StatusNegativeFill : BrandPalette.NeutralText;
```

So the buttons are enabled/disabled purely by whether the row is an Admin. An inactive non-admin employee still has an enabled Edit button, an enabled Reset Password button, and the Deactivate button shows "Reactivate Employee" (since `emp.IsActive` is false). That's the bug: only the label switched, not the enabled state.

**The rule you want:** when the selected employee is inactive, all buttons except Reactivate are disabled. When they're active, the existing rule applies (Admin → all disabled; non-Admin → all enabled).

That's a small change to `RefreshDrawer`. One patch.

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein/Views/Controls/ManageUsersView.cs`

**Search for:**

```csharp
            // The server blocks editing/deactivating Admin accounts. Grey out the buttons for that case.
            var isAdminRow = emp.Role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                 emp.Role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
            editBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow;
            resetPasswordBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow;

            // The "deactivate" button doubles as reactivate depending on the employee's current
            // state. Only admins' accounts are locked out entirely.
            deactivateBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow;
            deactivateBtn.Text = emp.IsActive ? "Deactivate Employee" : "Reactivate Employee";
            deactivateBtn.ForeColor = emp.IsActive
                ? BrandPalette.StatusNegativeFill
                : BrandPalette.NeutralText;
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // Two independent reasons to lock down an employee:
            //   1. The row is an Admin/SuperAdmin (server blocks all edits to those).
            //   2. The employee is deactivated — only Reactivate is allowed.
            //
            // A row can be both (an inactive Admin), in which case Reactivate is also
            // disabled, since even that action isn't permitted on an Admin account from
            // this console.
            var isAdminRow = emp.Role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                 emp.Role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
            var isInactive = !emp.IsActive;

            editBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow && !isInactive;
            resetPasswordBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow && !isInactive;

            // The deactivate button doubles as reactivate. It's enabled when:
            //   - the row isn't an Admin (server blocks those entirely)
            //   - AND (the employee is active (deactivate is a valid action)
            //           OR the employee is inactive (reactivate is the only valid action))
            // In practice that means: enabled whenever !isAdminRow.
            // Both branches disable it for Admin rows.
            deactivateBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow;

            deactivateBtn.Text = isInactive ? "Reactivate Employee" : "Deactivate Employee";
            deactivateBtn.ForeColor = isInactive
                ? BrandPalette.NeutralText
                : BrandPalette.StatusNegativeFill;
```

Wait — that's the same enabled logic as before. Let me re-read your requirement:

> *"deactivated employees' profile appearing in the leftmost screen, everything should be untouchable except the reactivate button."*

So for an **inactive employee**:

- Edit: disabled.
- Reset Password: disabled.
- Deactivate/Reactivate: **enabled** (because it's now the Reactivate action).

For an **active employee**:

- Edit: enabled (unless Admin).
- Reset Password: enabled (unless Admin).
- Deactivate: enabled (unless Admin).

So the change versus current is: when the employee is **inactive**, additionally disable Edit and Reset Password. The Deactivate/Reactivate button stays enabled — which is the current behavior — but only says "Reactivate Employee."

Let me rewrite to be explicit about that:

```csharp
            // Two independent reasons to lock down an employee:
            //   1. The row is an Admin/SuperAdmin — the server blocks all edits to those.
            //   2. The employee is deactivated — only the reactivate action is allowed.
            //
            // For an Admin row: everything is disabled, including the deactivate/reactivate
            // toggle, since the server blocks even that.
            // For a non-Admin inactive row: Edit and Reset Password are disabled, but the
            // toggle stays enabled so the Manager can reactivate.
            var isAdminRow = emp.Role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                 emp.Role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
            var isInactive = !emp.IsActive;

            editBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow && !isInactive;
            resetPasswordBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow && !isInactive;
            deactivateBtn.Enabled = !isAdminRow;

            deactivateBtn.Text = isInactive ? "Reactivate Employee" : "Deactivate Employee";
            deactivateBtn.ForeColor = isInactive
                ? BrandPalette.NeutralText
                : BrandPalette.StatusNegativeFill;
```

That's the correct logic. The edit path changed: `editBtn.Enabled` and `resetPasswordBtn.Enabled` now include `&& !isInactive`, so inactive employees can't be edited or have their password reset.

## One follow-up: does the API agree?

Client-side disabling is cosmetic. A curious Manager could still hit `PUT /employees/{id}` or `POST /employees/{id}/reset-password` directly and edit an inactive employee. **Do you want the API to enforce this too?**

- **Yes:** add an `IsActive` check in the API's `UpdateEmployee` and `ResetPassword`. Reject if the target is inactive.
- **No:** leave it. The UI gates it; a Manager has no reason to call the API directly.

My lean: **yes**, add the API check — one condition per endpoint, and it closes the same hole we closed for `LogFeedback` and `CreateCustomer`. But it's a small extra patch, so tell me if you want it in this pass or later.

```csharp
approvalSectionPanel.Visible = CanApprove;
```

So a Barista sees the request form, no approval panel. A Manager sees the approval panel, no request form. That's what we specified. **What specifically is wrong on the staff side?** Two readings:

That contradicts the earlier design where Baristas file requests, but if you've changed your mind, it's a one-line fix (`CanRequestAdjustment => false` for everyone).
- **(b)** Baristas should see the request form but it's *actually rendering* something wrong — e.g. the form is visible but the fields are wrong, or the panel is empty/partial.

**Problem 2 — Manager side:** the approval panel is visible but the Manager can still press buttons they shouldn't. Specifically:

2. Is the approval panel visible? (It shouldn't be.)

## What I think the actual fix is (pending your screenshots)

My best guess: **the panel visibility is right but the button enabled-state inside each panel isn't.** Concretely, in `RefreshDrawerAsync` you have:

```csharp
requestAmountNud.Value = 0;
requestReasonTxtBx.Text = string.Empty;
requestStatusLabel.Text = string.Empty;
UpdateSubmitRequestEnabled();
...
approveBtn.Enabled = false;
rejectBtn.Enabled = false;
```

And `UpdateSubmitRequestEnabled`:

```csharp
    requestAmountNud.Value != 0 &&
    !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(requestReasonTxtBx.Text);
```

If `CanRequestAdjustment` is false (Manager), `submitRequestBtn.Enabled` is false. But the panel `requestSectionPanel` is set to `Visible = CanRequestAdjustment`, which is false for Manager. So the whole panel should be hidden.

**Unless the panel is actually the one named differently in the designer, or there's a second panel.** Looking at the designer you sent earlier for `CustomerManagementView.Designer.cs`:

```csharp
drawerFlow.Controls.Add(approvalSectionPanel);
```

```csharp
{
```

The whole `drawerContentPanel` is hidden, which contains both panels. Fine.

If you're seeing the panels as *visible and interactive* after a customer is selected, then `Visible = CanRequestAdjustment` isn't taking effect — maybe the panels have child controls whose visible state isn't inherited properly, or the role check is returning the wrong value.

The `CanRequestAdjustment` check `Role?.Equals("Barista", ...) == true` should be false for a Manager, true for a Barista.

**Unless the role string has whitespace or different casing.** The `.Equals(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` handles casing. Whitespace would break it — `"Manager "` != `"Manager"`. That's a possibility but unlikely.

**提问：**

ok lets rephrase that, baristas see the request what i meant by the manager side is that if a customer is inactive, they see the points approval form or rather they can interact with it im debating whether to just disable pressing any other button OTHER THAN THE REACTIVATE button or just hide everything except the reactivate.

**回答：**

Now I understand. The problem is the same class of bug as the employee side — when a customer is **inactive**, the drawer still shows all the interactive panels (request form for Baristas, approval panel for Managers, Edit Customer button), and you want them locked down. The Reactivate button should be the only actionable thing.

Good question to debate. Let me lay out both options with the tradeoffs, because it's genuinely a design call.

## Option A — Disable everything except Reactivate

The panels stay visible but their controls become `Enabled = false`:

- Request form: amount, reason, submit button → disabled.
- Approval panel: approve, reject, notes → disabled.
- Edit Customer button → disabled.
- Deactivate (i.e. Reactivate) button → enabled, reads "Reactivate Customer."
- Grid selection still works, order history / ledger still scrollable.

**Pros:**

- The Manager / Barista can still *see* the customer's context — their points balance, their pending requests, their history — while the customer is deactivated.
- Reads as "this row is off, no actions until reactivated."
- Consistent with how Manage Users handles inactive employees: profile stays visible, Edit / Reset Password disabled, Reactivate enabled.

**Cons:**

- More controls to individually disable (each button + each input needs its `Enabled` flipped).
- A viewer can still see the disabled request form and wonder why it's there.

## Option B — Hide everything except Reactivate

The panels are hidden entirely for inactive customers:

- Request form: hidden.
- Approval panel: hidden.
- Edit Customer button: hidden.
- Deactivate/Reactivate button: visible, reads "Reactivate Customer."
- Profile box, order history, ledger: still visible (they're the customer's record; nothing wrong with reading them).

**Pros:**

- Cleaner. Nothing to disable; just don't show it.
- Reads unambiguously as "there's one thing you can do here."
- Less code than Option A — a couple of `Visible` toggles, no per-control `Enabled` fiddling.

**Cons:**

- The Manager can't see the pending requests for an inactive customer, which might matter if they want to know "did we owe this person points before deactivating them?"

## My recommendation

**Option B, with one refinement.** Hide the interactive panels (request form, approval panel, Edit Customer button). Leave the profile box, order history, ledger, and pending requests **grid** visible — the grid is read-only, and knowing a customer's outstanding point-adjustment requests is useful context before reactivating them.

So the visibility matrix for the drawer when `!customer.IsActive`:

| Element | Active customer | Inactive customer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Profile box | ✅ | ✅ |
| Status label | ✅ | ✅ |
| Request form (Barista only) | ✅ | ❌ hidden |
| Approval panel (Manager only) | ✅ | ❌ hidden |
| Edit Customer button (Manager only) | ✅ | ❌ hidden |
| Deactivate / Reactivate button (Manager only) | ✅ (says "Deactivate") | ✅ (says "Reactivate") |
| Order history grid | ✅ | ✅ |
| Ledger grid | ✅ | ✅ |
| Pending requests grid | ✅ | ✅ |

This matches the Manage Users pattern almost exactly: the profile is visible, most actions are gone or disabled, one button (Reactivate) remains.

## One question before I patch

You asked **"disable or hide"**. I'm proposing **hide** for the three interactive elements (request form, approval panel, Edit button) — nothing to disable, they just aren't there. And **keep visible** for the read-only context (profile, order history, ledger, pending requests).

**Does that match what you want?** Or do you want the panels visible-but-disabled (Option A) so the Manager can still see the request form as context even if they can't use it?

**One extra thing to consider:** if a Barista deactivates a customer (they can't — only Manager can deactivate) — actually they can't. So the request form being hidden for inactive customers only affects Baristas, and they never see inactive customers anyway (default filter is Active, no reason for them to flip it). So the request-form hiding is mostly a no-op for Baristas. The Manager's approval panel and Edit button are the ones that matter, and those are the ones you flagged.

Confirm **hide** vs **disable** and I'll write it as one patch.

Baristas: no change to their view because they never open an inactive customer. Even if they did, the request form isn't hidden for them by this patch — but that's moot.

## Patch — hide interactive panels for inactive customers

**File:** `CRM_Morcaffein/Views/Controls/CustomerManagementView.cs`

**Search for** (in `RefreshDrawerAsync`, the block that sets the panel visibilities):

```csharp
            requestSectionPanel.Visible = CanRequestAdjustment;
            approvalSectionPanel.Visible = CanApprove;

            // If the user was mid-edit and the drawer is being repopulated (row change,
            // page change, save), abandon the edit silently rather than carrying stale
            // text into a different customer.

                ExitCustomerEditState();

            _editCustomerBtn.Visible = CanEditCustomer;
            _deactivateCustomerBtn.Visible = CanEditCustomer;

            // Deactivate button doubles as Reactivate depending on the customer's state.
            // The negative text color is only appropriate for the destructive direction.

            _deactivateCustomerBtn.Text = customerIsActive
                ? "Deactivate Customer"
                : "Reactivate Customer";
```

**Replace with:**

```csharp
            // When the customer is inactive, the drawer becomes read-only: profile and
            // history remain visible, but every interactive element is hidden except the
            // Reactivate button. Matches how Manage Users locks down a deactivated employee.
            var customerIsActive = customer.IsActive;

            requestSectionPanel.Visible = CanRequestAdjustment && customerIsActive;
            approvalSectionPanel.Visible = CanApprove && customerIsActive;

            // If the user was mid-edit and the drawer is being repopulated (row change,
            // page change, save), abandon the edit silently rather than carrying stale
            // text into a different customer.
            if (_isEditingCustomer)
                ExitCustomerEditState();

            // Edit is only available on an active customer.
            _editCustomerBtn.Visible = CanEditCustomer && customerIsActive;

            // Deactivate/Reactivate stays visible for Managers regardless of state —
            // for an inactive customer it's the one actionable button.
            _deactivateCustomerBtn.Visible = CanEditCustomer;

            _deactivateCustomerBtn.Text = customerIsActive
                ? "Deactivate Customer"
                : "Reactivate Customer";
            _deactivateCustomerBtn.ForeColor = customerIsActive
                ? BrandPalette.StatusNegativeFill
                : BrandPalette.NeutralText;
```

**Two changes:**

1. `requestSectionPanel.Visible` and `approvalSectionPanel.Visible` now also require `customerIsActive`. Inactive → hidden for both roles (though only Manager ever lands here).
2. `_editCustomerBtn.Visible` now also requires `customerIsActive`. Inactive → hidden.

`_deactivateCustomerBtn` unchanged in visibility — always visible to Managers. Its label and text color still flip on state, as before.

**What stays visible for an inactive customer:** profile box, status line, order history grid, ledger grid, pending requests grid. All read-only. The Reactivate button is the only interactive control.

**One extra thing to check — do we need to reset the approval panel's internal state?**

`RefreshDrawerAsync` already resets `approvalHintLabel`, `approveBtn.Enabled`, `rejectBtn.Enabled`, `rejectionNotesTxtBx.Text`, and `approvalStatusLabel.Text` at the bottom of the method, unconditionally. That's fine — resetting a hidden panel is harmless.

Same for the request form's `submitRequestBtn.Enabled`, `requestAmountNud.Value`, `requestReasonTxtBx.Text` — all reset unconditionally at the bottom. Harmless when hidden.

So no additional reset needed.
